entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: o Either to the paths which lead to her House: or to her manner of living.

entries.title: Proverbs 7:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: p Men that excel others, either 1. in bodily strength, upo which they presume, which yet is wasted and by degrees ruined by these courses. Or. 2. in wisdom and fortitude and resolution. Whereby he implies how much more necessary it is for a weak and foolish young Man to use all possible care and diligence to avoid this mischief.

entries.title: Proverbs 7:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 18. [illegible] [illegible] 9. [illegible]

q Or, to the Grave; for the word is used in both senses; and this sense seems better to agree both with the foregoing and following words. Although, without repentance, Hell will certainly be their portion, and their first death will be followed by the second.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 20.

a It is a great Question what this Wisdom is, of which Solomon discourseth so largely and profoundly in this Chapter. Some understand it of that attribute or perfection of the Divine nature which is called Wisdom, whereby God perfectly knoweth all things, and maketh known to men what he judgeth necessary, or expedient for them to know. Others understand it o[illegible] the second Person in the Godhead, the Son of God, who is called the Wisdom of God, Luk. 11. 49. And it cannot fairly be denied that some passages do best agree to the former, and others to the latter Opinion. Possibly both may be joined together, and the Chapter may be understood of Christ considered partly in his Per[illegible]onal capacity and partly in regard of his Office which was to impart the mind and will of God to Mankind, which he did, 1. by revealing it to, and writing it upon the mind of Man, at his first Creation; for it was Christ who then gave being, and life, and [illegible]ight to Mankind, as is undeniably evident from Ioh. 1. 1, 2, 3, 4, &c. 2. By publishing it unto the holy Patriarchs and Prophets in the time of the Old Testament; for it was Christ who spake and discovered things to them from time to time, as is manifest from 1 Pet. 1. 11. & 3. 18 19, 20. and from many other Scriptures both of the Old Testament, as I have formerly noted in their proper places, and in the New Testament, as we shall see hereafter. 3. By declaring it from his own mouth and by his Apostles and Ministers under the Gospel.

b Clearly and audibly instruct men how to avoid those fleshly lusts? He opposeth the inviting words of VVisdom to the seducing speeches of the Harlot.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c VVhere she may be best seen and heard, not in corners and in the dark, as the Harlot did.

d VVhere many paths meet, where there is a great concourse, and where Travellers may need direction.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e The places of Judgment, and of the confluence of People.

f To invite Passengers at their first coming, and to conduct them to her House.

g To wit, of her House, as the Harlot stood at her Door to invite Lovers.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, O great men. Ps. 62, 9.

Or, to mean men.

h To all men without exception, even to the meanest, who are thus called, Psal. 49. 2.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i VVho want knowledge and experience, and are easily deceived.

Heb. subtilty.

k Wilful and obstinate Sinners.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. princely things.

l Heb. of Princely things: worthy of Princes to learn and practice them. Or, such as excel common things as much as Princes do ordinary Persons.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Heb. shall meditate, i. e. shall speak not rashly, and hastily, but what I have well considered and digested.

Heb. the abomination of my lips.

n I hate to speak it; therefore you may be assured that I shall not deceive you.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o All my Precepts, Promises, Threatnings, &c.

Heb. wreathed.

p Not the least mixture of vanity, or error, or folly in them, as there is in the words of the wisest Philosophers, &c.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q Evident and clear to their minds or, right, just and good

r Either to him who with an honest mind applies himself to the study of them in the diligent use of all the means appointed by God to that end: or to him whose mind God hath enlightned by his Spirit, though they seem otherwise to ignorant and carnal-minded men.

s That are truely wise and discerning Persons and taught of God.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: s i. e. Rather than Silver, as such negative expressions are understood, Gen. 45. 8. Exod. 16. 8. Ier. 7. 22. & 16. 14, 15. and in many other places. Though withal he seems to intimate the inconsistency of these two studies and designs, and the great hinderance which the love of Riches gives to the study of Wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, subtilty.

t I do not content my self with high Speculations, but my unseparable Companion is Prudence to govern all my own actions and to direct the actions of others, by good counsels. This he saith, because some Persons have much wit and knowledge, and nothing of discretion.

u i. e. I know them as clearly and certainly as if I had found them out by diligent searching. Or, I find out, is put for I help men to find out, as the Spirit is said to intercede, Rom. 8. 26. when it helpeth us to do so.

x Of all ingenious designs and contrivances for the service and glory of God, and for the good of our selves and others. But why may it not be rendred, of wicked devices, as this very word is translated, Prov. 12. 2. & 14. 17. & 24. 8. For surely this is one great work of Prudence to discover and so avoid all evil counsels or devices, and the effects of them But this I propose with submission, because I have not the concurrence of any Interpreter in this Exposition.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y Which he had before noted to be the beginning of Wisdom Ch. 1. 7.

z It consists in a careful abstinence from all sin, and that not from carnal or prudential Motives, but from a true dislike and hatred of it.

a Which he mentions first as that which is most hateful to God, and most opposite to true Wisdom and to the fear of God, which constantly produce humility.

b All wicked actions, especially sinful customs and courses.

c False Doctrines, and bad Counsels and Deceits.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d All solid and substantial and usefull, yea essential Wisdom is natural and essential to me, for the word properly signifies essence.

e By my nature and essence, as was now said. Or, I am the Author of Understanding; as Iob. 17. 3. This is life Eternal i. e. this is the cause or means of it.

Heb. strength is mine.

f Courage and resolution to execute all my Counsels and to conquer all difficulties.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Dan. 2. 21. Rom. 13. 1.

g Either 1. They get their Kingdoms by mine appointment and providence. Or rather 2. they rule their Kingdoms wisely, and justly, and happily by my counsel and assistance. For this best suits with the next Clause.

h Their injustice or wickedness is from themselves, but all the just and good things which they do, they owe to my conduct.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i I do not despise their love, though it be but a small and inconsiderable thing to me, but I kindly accept it and will recompence it with my love and favour.

Jam. 1. 5.

k i. e. With sincere affection, and great diligence, and above all other persons or things in the world. VVhich he mentions as the effect and evidence of their love: for otherwise all men pretend to love God.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 3. 16.

l Which he mentions here either 1. as the best and surest way to get and to keep Riches, for Estates unjustly gotten quickly vanish, as is manifest both from Scripture and from common observation. Or 2. to signifie that this Wisdom gives both Worldly, and Spiritual or Heavenly Blessings together to its followers, whereas God gives Riches alone to ungodly men, and they are to expect no other Portion.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, walk.

m Keeping at an equal distance from both extreams, and from the very borders of them: which is called a putting away iniquity far from us, Job 22. 23.

entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: n Substantial, and true, and satisfying happiness: which is here opposed to all worldly enjoyments, which are said not to be, Prov. 23 5. which are but meer shadows and dreams of felicity.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o As his Son by Eternal Generation, who was from Eternity with him, as is said, Ioh. 1. 1. and in him as he also was in me, Joh. 14 10.

p Yea and before the beginning, as it is largely expressed in the following Verses.

q Either 1. of his counsels or decrees. Or rather 2. of his works of Creation, as it follows.

entries.title: Proverbs 8:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r Heb. anointed, ordained or constituted to be the Person by whom the Father resolved to do all his works, first to create, and then to uphold and govern and judge, and afterwards to redeem and save the world; all which works are particularly ascribed to the Son of God, as is manifest from, Ioh. 1. 1. &c. Col. 1. 16, 17. Heb. 1. 3. and many other places, as we may see hereafter in their several places.

u No abyss or deep Waters either mixed with the Earth, as they were at first, or separated from it.

Gen. 1. 9, 1[illegible] Job 38. 1[illegible] [illegible]1. Ps. 1[illegible]4. 9. Jer. 5. 22.

entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a For the reception and entertainment of her Guests, as appears from the following passages. This house is opposed to the Harlots House mentioned, Prov. 7. 8. and it is to be understood, either 1. of the heavenly House or the Palace of Glory: Or rather 2. of the Church which Christ, the Wisdom of the Father, hath erected and established in the World, in which this following Feast is made, which is called God's House, 1 Tim. 3. 15. Heb. 3. 3, 4.

c Prophets, and Apostles, and Ministers of Holy things, which, in Scripture are called Pillars, as Gal. 2. 9. and elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Matth. 22. [illegible].

Heb. [illegible] [illegible].

e Either 1. with Spices, to make it strong and delightful, this mixed Wine being mentioned as the best, Prov. 23. 29, 30. Or 2. with Water, as they used to do in those hot Countries, partly for refreshment, and partly for wholesomness. Whereby also may be intimated that Wisdom teacheth us temperance in the use of our comforts.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:

Ch. 8. 2.

Heb. [illegible] [illegible] of the [illegible] places

entries.title: Proverbs 9:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i Ignorant, and weak, and subject to delusion and willing to learn: to shew that Wisdom rejects those Scholars who are proud and self conceited.

k Heb. heart, which signifies understanding, Ier. 5. 21. Hos. 7. 11.

entries.content: [illegible]ant. 5. 1. [illegible] 55. 1.

entries.content:
l i. e. The wicked, and their courses and society: you must either forsake them or me, for we are irreconcilable enemies.

m Which leads to it and is prescribed by it.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n The connexion may be conceived thus, Having invited the simple, he forbids the invitation of scorners: Or thus, He sheweth who he meant by the foolish, v. 6. even scorners and wicked men, as they are here called, and he presseth his last advice of forsaking them because there was no good, but hurt to be got by conversation with them.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]at. 7. 6.

s Who is opposed to the Scorner, to intimate that Scorners, howsoever they are thought by themselves or others to be witty or wise, yet in God's account, and in truth, are fools.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 1. 5.

x Called a wise Man in the former branch; to intimate that good men are the onely wise men.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 28. 28. Ps. 111. 10. Chap. 1. 7.

y Either 1. of holy men, whether such as all Saints learn or rather such as the holy men of God, the Servants of this Wisdom, teach from God's VVord: Or rather 2. of Holy things the Hebrew word being here taken in the Neuter Gender, as it is Numb. 5. 17. and elsewhere: for this seems best to answer to the fear of the Lord in the other branch.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Thou dost not profit me, but thy self by it: I advise thee for thine own good.

Heb. and.

b The blame and mischief of it falls wholly upon thee, not upon me or my VVord or Ministers who have warned thee.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 7. 11.

c By which he understands, either 1. folly, which is opposite to that VVisdom of which he hath been so long discoursing, and so it may include all wickedness, either in principle, as Idolatry, Heresy, &c. or in practice. Or 2. the Harlot: which with submission, seems most probable to me, partly because all the following decription exactly agrees to her, especially what is said, v. 17. as also v. 18. which in effect was said of the Harlot before, Ch. 2. 18. & 5. 5. and partly because such transitions from discoursing of VVisdom, to a discourse of Harlots are frequent in Solomon, as we have seen Ch. 2. 16. & 5. 3. & 7. 5.

d Speaks loudly that she may be heard and vehemently that Persons might be moved by her persuasions.

e To wit, aright, nothing that is good, nothing for her good, though she be subtil in little artifices for her own wicked ends.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: f Which notes her idleness and impudence and diligence in watching for occasions of sin.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: g Who were going innocently and directly about their business without any unchast design; for others needed none of those invitations or offers, but went to her of their own accord. And besides such leud Persons take a greater pleasure in corrupting the innocent.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: h Which title is not given to them by her, for such a reproach would not have allured them, but driven them away but by Solomon who represents the matter of her invitation in his own words that he might discover the truth of the business, and thereby dissuade and deter those whom she invited.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 2[illegible]. 17.

i By which he understandeth, either 1. Idolatry or other wickednesses, which in Solomon's time before his fall were publickly forbidden and punished, but privately practised. Or rather 2. Adultery.

k Partly from the difficulty of obtaining them; partly from the art which men use in contriving such secret sins; and partly because the very prohibition renders it more grateful to corrupt Nature.

Heb. of secrecies.

entries.title: Proverbs 9:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: l i. e. He doth not consider it seriously, whereby he proveth his folly.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Properly so called, for the foregoing Chapters, though they had this Title in the beginning of them, yet in truth were only a Preface or preparation to them, containing a general Exhortation to the study and exercise of wisdom, to stir up the minds of men to the greater attention and regard to all its Precepts, whereof some here follow. Of which in general these things are fit to be observed, to help us in the understanding of them: 1. That these sentences are generally distinct and independent, having no coherence one with another, as many other parts of Scripture have: 2. That such sentences being very short, as their nature requires, more is understood in them than is expressed, and the Causes are commonly to be gathered from the Effects, and the Effects from the Causes, and one opposite from another, as we shall see. 3. That they are delivered by way of comparison and opposition, which for the most part is between Virtue and Vice, but sometimes is between two Virtues, or two Vices.

b i. e. Prudent, and especially virtuous and godly, as this word is commonly meant in this Book, and in many other Scriptures.

‖ Ch. 15. 20.

c And a glad Mother too; for both Parents are to be understood in both branches, as is evident from the nature of the thing which affects both of them, and from parallel places, as Ch. 17. 25. & 30. 17. although one only be expressed in each branch, for the greater Elegancy.

d The occasion of her great sorrow, which is decently ascribed to the Mothers, rather than to the Fathers, because their passions are most vehement, and make deepest impression in them.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 11. 4.

e Either 1. All worldly Treasures and Riches, which are called the Mammon of Unrighteousness, Luke 16. 9. of which see the Reasons there, to which Righteousness or Holiness, which are spiritual and heavenly Riches, may be fitly opposed. Or 2. Such Treasures as are got by any sort of unjust or wicked practices.

f They do the possessor no good, but, which is implied from the opposite member, much hurt; they do not only not deliver him from death, but oft expose him to it, either from men, who take away his Life that they may enjoy his Wealth, or from God, who shortens his days, and makes his death more terrible, as being attended with guilt, and with the second death.

g Either 1. True Holiness of Heart and Life. Or 2. Justice and Equity in the getting of Riches, or an Estate honestly obtained, which may be fitly opposed to Treasures of Wickedness. Or 3. A liberal and charitable use of Riches, which is oft called Righteousness, as Psal. 112. 9. Dan. 4. 27. 2 Cor. 9. 10. &c. and is indeed but an act of Justice, of which see on Prov. 3. 27. which also is conveniently opposed to an unjust getting of Riches; and so this contains a great Paradox, yet a certain truth, that the charitable laying out of Mony is more profitable to men than an unjust and covetous laying it up.

h Oft times from temporal death, because men generally love, and honour, and will assist such persons in cases of danger, and God gives them the blessing of a long Life; and always from eternal death, when such Charity proceeds from a sincere and honest mind, and a good Conscience.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 33. 19, & 37. 19, 25.

i Will preserve them from Famine, according to his Promises, Psal. 34. 10. and elsewhere, which, as other temporal Promises, is not to be understood simply and universally, but with this limitation, except this be necessary for Gods Glory, which in all reason should over-rule the Creatures good, and for their own greater benefit. For to say nothing of eternal Felicities which follow every good mans death, it is certainly in some times and cases, a less evil for men to be killed with Famine, than to survive to see and feel those miseries which are coming upon them, and upon the Land where they live.

Or, the wicked for their wickedness.

k As this word is used, Psal. 52. 7. or the Wickedness, i. e. the wealth gotten by wickedness, as Righteousness, v. 2. is by divers understood of an Estate got with Righteousness.

l Who by that means shall be exposed to want and Famine.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12 24. & 19. 15.

m Negligently and slothfully, as appears from the diligence opposed to it in the next branch, and from the use of this word in this sense, Prov. 12. 24, 27. & 19. 15. Ier. 48. 10. Heb. with a deceitful hand, so called, partly because it seems and pretends to do somthing, when in truth it doth nothing; and partly because such persons usually endeavour to maintain themselves by deceit and wickedness, which they cannot or will not do by honest labour and diligence.

Chap. 13. 4. & 21. 5.

n Not by it self, nor necessarily, as is manifest from Experience, and is noted, Eccles. 9. 11. but through Gods blessing, which commonly is given to such, by comparing this verse with v. 22. here following.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o The fruits of his field.

p In harvest, as it follows, which is a part of Summer. He that watcheth for and improveth the proper seasons and opportunities of doing good to himself, and to others.

q Both to himself for his folly, and that Poverty and Misery caused by it, and to his Parents, to whose negligent or evil Education such things are oft, and somtimes justly imputed.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r All sorts of blessings are wished to them by Men, and conferred upon them by God. He saith, upon their head, either to shew that these Blessings come from above: and that openly in the sight of the World, so that he can confidently speak of them to God's Praise, and to his own Comfort and Honour; or because Blessings were commonly pronounced by men with this Ceremony by laying their hands upon the Head of the party blessed.

Ver. 11.

s Violence (either 1. Their own Violence or Injustice, which may be here put for the fruit or punishment of it, as Iniquity is oft put for the punishment of Iniquity. Or 2. Violence, or the violent and injurious, and mischievous practices of others against them, deserved by their own Violence committed against others, and inflicted upon them by the curse and righteous judgment of God) shall cover the mouth of the wicked, i. e. shall fall upon them. This Phrase of covering their Mouth, is used either 1. With allusion to the ancient custom of covering the Mouths and Faces of condemned Malefactors; of which see Esth. 7. 8. Iob 9. 24. Or 2. To signifie that the Curse and Judgment of God upon them should be so manifestly just, that their mouths should be stopped, and they not be able to speak a word against God, or for themselves. Or 3. to intimate that Gods judgment upon them should be publick and evident to all that behold them, as any covering put upon a mans mouth or Face is, as for the same reason the blessings of the just were said to be upon their Heads. And the Mouth may be put for the Face, or Countenance, by a Synecdoche: But this clause is otherwise rendred by divers learned Interpreters, the mouth of the wicked covereth (i. e. concealeth or smothereth within itself, and doth not utter that) violence or injury, which he meditateth in his Heart, and designeth to do to others, and therefore shall be accursed and miserable. But this suits not so well with the former clause, wherein the Blessings of the just are not meant actively of those Blessings which they wish or give to others, but passively of those Blessings which others wish or give to them, and consequently this violence is not understood of that which they do to others, but of that which is done to them by others.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 112. 6.

t i. e. Honourable and acceptable to those who mention them. Compare Iob 31. 20. Psal. 62. 5.

u Shall perish, and be cursed and detestable amongst men, shall stink above ground.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
x Is ready to hear and obey the Counsels and Precepts of God and of Men, by which means he shall stand fast and live.

Heb. a fool of lips.

y One who is slow to hear, and swift to speak, who instead of receiving good Admonitions, Cavils, and Disputes against them. In the Hebrew he is called a fool of Lips, either because he discovers the folly of his Heart by his Lips, and thereby exposeth himself to the mischief here following, or because he is without heart, as is said of Ephraim, Hos. 7. 11. or, his Heart is little worth, as is said here, v. 20. or because he speaks rashly without any consideration. Or, it may be rendred, a fool by his lips, i. e. by his foolish and wicked speeches, contrary to the commands of God, by talking much and ill, when it is more comely and necessary for him to hear and receive Instruction from others.

Or, shall be beaten.

z To wit, into mischief: or, be punished, as the word is used, Hos. 4. 14. or, be beaten, as below v. 10.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 23. 4.

a Who is sincere, and just, and faithful in his dealings with God and with men.

b Or, securely, or confidently, as the word properly signifies, and is here rendred by all the ancient Interpreters, and by most of the others, quietly resting upon Gods Favour, and gracious Providence for his Protection, and being supported by the Testimony of a good Conscience, and therefore not fearing nor caring who knows or observes his Actions, which he endeavours to approve both to God, and to men.

c That walks perversly, or frowardly, or in crooked and sinful paths, that dealeth hypocritically and deceitfully with God, or with men, using all possible crafts to conceal his wickedness.

d His wickedness shall be publickly discovered, and so he shall be exposed to all that shame and punishment which his sins deserve, and which he thought by his cunning practices to avoid.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 6. 13.

e That secretly and cunningly designs mischiefs against others, as this Phrase is used, Psal. 35. 19. Prov. 6. 13.

f To others, and afterwards to himself.

g Or, and, as it is in the Hebrew: for vice is not here opposed to virtue, as it is in many other Proverbs, but one vice is compared with another.

Ver. 8.

h Who is so far from such deceits, that he runs into the other extream, and uttereth all his mind, as is said of the Fool, Prov. 29. 11. and thereby speaks many things offensive to others, and mischievous to himself.

Or, shall be beaten.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] [illegible]7. 30, [illegible] Ch 14. 14.

i Continually sending forth Waters of Life, or such good and wholsom words, as are very refreshing and useful both to themselves and others, for the preserving of their natural Life and for the promoting of their Spiritual and eternal Life. We have the same Phrase, Psal 36. 9.

[illegible]. 6.

k The same words were used before, v. 6. where see the Notes; and they may be understood in the same sense here, and the opposition of this clause to the former, may be conceived thus: As the Mouth of a good man speaketh those things which are good and beneficial to himself and others, so the Mouth of the wicked uttereth violence, or injury, or things injurious to others, which at last fall upon himself. But it is no new thing for the same words and Phrases to be taken in different senses, in the same Chapter, and somtimes in the same verse, as Matth. 8. 22. and elsewhere; and therefore these words may here be, and are, by many translated and interpreted thus, the mouth of the wicked covereth (i. e. concealeth) violence or mischief, which he plotteth against others. And so here is a double opposition between the Righteous and the wicked; first in the contrary effects, the former causeth Life, the latter mischief and death; and secondly in the manner of producing them, the righteous doth it by uttering his words, and the wicked doth it by concealing his mind.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
l Upon every sleight occasion, by filling men with suspicions and surmises, whereby they imagine faults where there are none, and aggravate every small offence.

[illegible] Cor. 13. 4. [illegible] 4. 8.

m Either doth not severely observe, or doth willingly forget and forgive the Offences or Injuries of others, and so preventeth contention and mischief.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n His Wisdom sheweth itself in his prudent speeches, by which he escapeth that rod which fools m[illegible] with, and gaineth that Reputation and Advantage to himself which Fools lose.

Chap. 29. 3.

o He may expect Rebukes and Punishments from God and men.

[illegible]. [illegible].

p Which he sheweth by his foolish words.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q To wit, in their minds and memories, to be brought forth thence upon fit occasions.

r Whereby they may be enabled to speak both what, and when it is seasonable, for their own or others good.

Chap. 13. 3.

s Fools are more forward to lay out than to lay up, and for want of knowledge speak much and foolishly, whereby they frequently bring destruction upon themselves.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 18. 11.

t Either 1. really, as money is called a defence, Eccl. 7. 12. because it oft-times redeems a man from Dangers and Calamities. Or 2. in his own conceit, as it is explained, and fully expressed, Ch. 18. 11. It makes him secure and confident.

u It is the cause of their ruine. Or, the contrition, or the terrour, or consternation, as others, both ancient and modern, render it. Their Poverty takes away their Spirit and Courage, and fills them with Fear and Despair.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 11. 30.

x Either 1. the design of his labour is only this, that he may have wherewith to live honestly, without sinful shifts. Or 2. the fruit or effect of his labour or industry (as this word, labour, is most commonly understood, and this best answers to the following clause, where fruit is put instead of this labour) is the preservation, and prolongation of this Life, and the obtaining of eternal Life, to which an honest and consciencious Diligence in mens worldly Callings doth in some manner contribute.

y The fruit of all their Labours and endeavours.

z Tendeth to sin, serves only for fuel to mens Pride, and Luxury, and Worldliness, and by that means oft causeth Temporal, and always, without Repentance, Eternal Death.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 6. 23.

a Which leadeth to Life and Blessedness.

b That observeth and obeyeth the wholsom Counsels of God, and of good men.

Or, causeth [illegible].

b To wit, from the way of Life, or into the ways of sin, and so of Death. Heb. leadeth into errour, or seduceth, to wit, himself, as appears by the opposition of this to the former clause; he wittingly and willingly exposeth himself to Temptation and Wickedness, because he rejecteth that Admonition which is a proper Preservative from it.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d With flattering words and false pretences of Friendship.

e Heb. he, i. e. both of them, one no less than the other. So he condemneth two opposite vices, secret Hatred, and manifest slander.

f Because a sinner, and because the mischief of these things will fall upon himself.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Men that love and commonly use much talking, do frequently run into many miscarriages, because such persons, for the most part, want Wisdom to order their words aright, Eccles. 5. 3. and speak hastily without care and consideration.

h That forbeareth to utter what cometh into his mind, before he hath weighed whether it be true, and fit to be spoken, or not.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i Of great worth and use, bringing credit to himself, and much benefit to others.

k And consequently the Tongue, which speaketh out of the abundance of the Heart, Mat. 12. 34.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
l By their wise and pious Discourses, Counsels, and Comforts, which are so many evidences of their Wisdom.

Heb. of heart.

m They have not Wisdom to feed or preserve themselves, much less to feed others.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n Riches are not got by Wisdom or diligence, but only by Gods Favour and Blessing.

o i. e. with that blessing which gives Riches, but gives them content and comfort in their Riches, which is a singular gift and blessing of God, of which see Eccles. 2. 24. 26. & 3. 13. & 5. 17, 18. whereas the Riches which wicked men get, are attended with Gods Curse, with many discontents, with tormenting cares and fears, with horrours of Conscience, and with the just dread of a sad account to God for them.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 14. 9. & 15. 21.

p He doth it with ease and delight, and without any shame, or remorse, or fear.

q Or, as others, to work wickedness, yea, great and premeditated wickedness, as the Hebrew word properly signifies.

r Whereby he is kept from committing Wickedness, and especially from sporting himself with it. But this clause is by divers learned Interpreters rendred thus, and, or so is Wisdom to a man of Understanding, it is a sport or pleasure to him to practice Wisdom or Piety. Which Translation makes the Opposition more evident.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
s The evils which he feareth, or hath cause to fear, as fear is oft taken.

t God will not only prevent the mischiefs which they fear, but grant them the good things which they desire.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u Which is suddenly, though with great noise and violence.

x His Power and Felicity is lost in an instant.

Chap. 12. 3, 7. Mat. 7. 24, 25. & 16. 18.

y Or, hath an everlasting, &c. His hope and Happiness is built upon a sure and unmoveable Foundation.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Unserviceable and vexatious.

z Which by its cold and sharpness it offends.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 9. 11.

Heb. addeth.

b Partly because it gives them a title to the Promise of long life, as well as to other Promises; partly because it gladdeth the heart, which doth good like a Medicine, Prov. 17. 22. and preserves a man from those wicked practices which tend to the shortning of the days.

Job 15. 32. & 22. 16. Psal. 55. 23.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Though at present it be mixed with doubts, and fears, and disappointments, yet at last it shall be accomplished, and turned into enjoyment.

Job 8. 13. & 11 20. Psal. 112. 10.

d Shall be utterly frustrated. and so end in sorrow.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e Either 1. The way or course of Gods Providence in the government of the world. Or rather 2. The way of Gods Precepts, as Gods way or ways are most commonly understood in Scripture, or walking in Gods ways; for this is opposed to working iniquity in the next clause.

f Gives strength, i. e. either courage and confidence: or support and protection from that destruction here following.

g Or, terrour or consternation, as the word properly signifies, and many render it. The design of this verse is to shew that Piety is the only true Policy.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 37. 22. & 125. 1.

h They shall live long and happily here, when this is most expedient for them, and eternally in Heaven.

i They shall not have so much as a long and quiet abode upon Earth, unless where this is a Curse and Mischief to them, and much less shall they have any possession in Heaven.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 37. 30.

k Freely, and abundantly, and constantly, as the Earth or a Tree bring forth their proper fruit, as the word properly signifies.

l Wise Counsels, by which he directeth and secureth himself and others.

m Because it bringeth forth not Wisdom, but Folly and Wickedness.

entries.title: Proverbs 10:32
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n To wit, practically, so as to consider and speak. Knowledg is here ascribed to the Lips, as it is to the Hands, Psal. 78. 72. because they are conducted by knowledg and Wisdom.

o To God and good men, or what is truly worthy of acceptation; for this is opposed to what is froward or wicked in the next clause.

Heb. frowardnesses.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Lev. 19. 35, 36. Deut. 25. 13, 15, 16. Chap. 16. 11. & 20. 10, 23.

Heb. ballances of deceit.

a The use of all false weights and measures in commerce.

b i. e. Highly abominable, as the abstract signifies; which is opposed to the false opinion of men who account it a fineness of wit, or, at worst, but a trivial fault.

c Partly because this wickedness is acted under a colour of Justice; and partly because it is destructive to humane Society, and especially to the poor, whose Patron the Lord owneth himself to be.

Heb. perfect stone.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 15. 33. & 16. 18. & 18. 12.

d Pride, as it is the effect of Folly, so it bringeth a man to contempt and destruction, such persons being commonly hated both by God, and by all men.

e Whereby they are kept from those foolish and wicked actions which expose men to shame.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 13. 6.

f Their sincere Obedience to Gods Laws.

g Shall keep them from crooked and dangerous courses, and lead them in a right and safe way.

h Those wicked devices by which they design and expect to secure themselves, shall be the instrument of their destruction.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 10. 3. Ezek. 7. 19. Zeph. 1. 18.

i In the time of Gods Judgments, when he is executing Wrath and Vengeance upon Sinners.

k Or, Mercy, as this word is oft rendred, or Charity to the poor, which is fitly opposed to Riches laid up in store.

l It moveth God to deliver them oft times from temporal Calamities, and always from eternal Death, where such actions are done from a right Principle.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. [illegible].

m Shall bring all his designs and endeavours to an happy issue, by comparing this clause with the next.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n From many snares and dangers.

Chap. 5. 22.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o All his hope and felicity, which he placed wholly in earthly things, is lost and gone with him.

p So it is a repetition of the same thing in other words. Or, as divers render it, the hope of their strengths, i. e. which they place in their carnal strengths, their Riches, Children, Friends, &c. So this is added by way of aggravation.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 21. 18.

q Is by Gods Providence brought into the same miseries which either he designed against the Righteous, or had formerly inflicted upon the Righteous, and now lately removed from them.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r By his corrupt communication, whereby he endeavours to draw him to errour or wickedness.

s To wit, of God, and of his word, which makes men wise, and discovers, and so prevents the frauds of Deceivers.

t From the infection of the Hypocrites evil and crafty Counsel.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u When such men are encouraged and advanced into places of Power and Trust.

x The Citizens or Subjects of that Government rejoyce, because they confidently expect Justice, and Tranquillity, and many other benefits, by their administration of publick affairs.

y A common rejoicing, partly for the just vengeance of God upon them who have been the instruments of so much mischief, and partly for their deliverance from such publick grievances and burdens of the Land.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
z Wherewith they bless the City, to wit, by their sincere Prayers, and wise and wholsom Counsels.

a By their Curses, and Oaths, and Blasphemies, and wicked and pernicious Counsels, whereby they both provoke God, and mislead men to their own ruine.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. destitute of heart.

b Which contempt he sheweth, either 1. by contemptuous or reproachful expressions of him; or 2. by not asking, or not regarding his advice, but trusting wholly to his own understanding.

c Either 1. He forbeareth all such expressions against his neighbour. Or 2 He silently and patiently bears these Reproaches from his neighbour, and doth not render one Reproach for another; wherein he sheweth true Wisdom. Or 3. He desireth and hearkeneth to the Counsels of others. Any of these ways the opposition is sufficiently evident.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. [illegible]e that walketh, b[illegible]ing a tale-bearer.

d Or, He that goeth about (from one place or person to another, as the manner of such is) telling tales, making it his business to scatter Reports.

e This tatling humour is so prevalent with him, that he cannot forbear to publish, either his neighbours secret faults, or such things as were committed to his trust with a charge of secrecy.

f That hath a sincere, and constant, and faithful mind, which both can and will govern his Tongue.

g So far as he can lawfully do.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
1 Kin. 12. 1. &c. Pro. 15. 22.

h Or, No wise counsel, as the word properly signifies, as Iob 37. 12. Prov. 1. 5.

i To wit, of wise and good Counsellors, for such will employ and unite their Counsels together for the publick good.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k Whose condition he doth not throughly understand, and therefore knows not his own danger.

[illegible] be [illegible].

[illegible]

l Of which see on Prov. 6. 1.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Heb, a Woman of grace and favour, i. e. one who by her meekness, and modesty, and prudence, and other Vertues renders her self acceptable and amiable to God and to men.

n Or, holdeth fast her honour, or good reputation, with no less care and resolution, than strong men do Riches, as it here follows.

o Or, as; for so this conjunction is o[illegible]t used in this Book, of which we have seen some, and may afterward see more instances.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p i. e. To himself, because his liberality shall turn to his own infinite advantage both in this life, and in the next.

q Hardhearted and uncharitable to others.

r Either 1. his own Children or Kindred, who are commonly expressed by this very word, for whose sakes he is thus covetous and uncharitable, that he may hoard it up for them: but they, faith the wise Man, shall have nothing but trouble and vexation, and God's curse with it. Or 2. himself denominated here from his flesh or Body as in the former Branch from his Soul. But he may seem to mention his flesh rather than his Soul, to intimate that the mischiefs of his covetousness shall not onely fall upon his Soul, which he despiseth, but upon his Flesh or outward Man, which is the onely thing that he feareth.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
s A work which will deceive his expectation of that good for which he worketh.

t That worketh it with constancy, and diligence, and hope of recompence, as they do who sow in Seed-time.

u Good works, acts of Piety towards God, and Charity to men.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: x Who are not over-taken by sin, as a good Man may be, Gal. 6. 1. but studiously design it, and follow after the occasions of it earnestly, and greedily, and industriously.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y Hypocrites, as appears from the opposition of these to the upright in the next Clause: whose Hearts are false to God, and contrary to their own professions.

z Though by their cunning Artifices they may deceive men, and gain their good opinion and favour, yet God sees their naughty Hearts and ha[illegible]eth them.

a In the course of their lives and actions. By which changing of the Phrase, from Heart in the first Clause, to way here, he intimates that the sincerity and hypocrisie of mens hearts are discovered, and to be judged by their conversations.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 16. 5.

b Though they are fortified against God's judgments by a numerous Issue and Kindred, and Friends, and by mutual strong combinations or con[illegible]ederacies.

c They shall be punished even in their own Persons, as well as in their Posterity. They shall not be able either totally to prevent God's judgment, or to delay it from coming in their days.

d Not onely their Persons, but their Children.

e Without any such Auxiliaries, by God's special Providence.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Which would not adorn the Swine, but onely be disparaged it self. It was the custom of some of the Iews to wear Jewels upon their Noses, and some of their Neighbours wore them in their Noses.

Heb. depar [illegible] [illegible].

g Which disgraceth the beauty of her Body by a foolish and filthy Soul.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: h Either 1 properly so called. So the sense is, His desires are generally and constantly to do good to men, as wicked mens designs are to do hurt, and to execute wrath and hatred against them. Or rather 2. the object, or event, or effect of their desire, as appears from the next Clause, where expectation is clearly put for the object or event of it: And the sense of the Proverb seems to be this, The desires and expectations of the Righteous shall end in their good and happiness, but the desires and expectations of wicked men shall be sadly disappointed, and end in the wrath of God, and their utter ruine.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i That giveth liberally of his Goods to the Poor: for so this Hebrew word is used, Psal. 112. 9. He hath dispersed, which is explained in the following words, he hath given to the Poor.

k Through God's secret Blessing upon his Estate.

l Heb. from what is right or just, i. e. what by the Law of God, and the Rules of general Justice, he is obliged to give: of which see Prov. 3. 27.

m By God's Providence secretly blasting his Estate, either in his own or his Childrens hands, as it very frequently befals covetous Wretches.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
2 Cor. 9. 8, 9, 10.

Heb. the soul of blessing.

n Heb. the Soul of Blessing, that man who is a Blessing to others, who blesseth them, i. e. doth good to them, as Blessing is oft used for a gift, as Gen. 33. 11. 1 Sam. 25. 27. 2 Cor. 9. 5.

o Shall be greatly enriched both with Temporal and Spiritual blessings.

p Possibly it is a Metaphor from a Fountain, which when it poureth forth its waters is instantly filled again, whereas if it be stopped it groweth empty and the Water seeketh another course. Others render it, he shall be a Rain, i. e. he shall receive such liberal supplies from God that he shall be able to pour forth showers of good things upon others.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q In a time of scarcity, when others need and desire it.

Amos 8. 5 6.

r The blessing of God which the People shall heartily beg for him.

s Upon reasonable terms.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t Which is opposed to those who content themselves with lazy desires or cold and careless endeavours.

Ch. 14. 22.

x With God and men.

Ps. 7. 15, 16. & 9. 15, 16. & 10. 2. & 57. 6.

y To do any mischief or injury to others.

z It shall be requi[illegible]ed either by mens malice and revenge, or by God's just judgment.

u To do good to all men, as he hath opportunity.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 31. 24.

a As his chief portion, and felicity, and ground of safety.

b As a withered Leaf, by comparing this Clause with the latter.

Ps. 1. 3. & 92. 12, &c. Jer 17. 8.

c Who maketh God alone, and not riches, his trust.

d To wit a green and flourishing branch.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e He who bringeth trouble and misery upon himself and Children, either 1. by carelesness, [illegible]lothfulness, improvidence, prodigality, or any wickedness, whereby he consumeth his Estate. So this troubling of his House may be opposed to a Man's building of his House, Jer. 29. 28. Or 2. by covetous desires and restless endeavours to heap up Riches, whereby he greatly tires and troubles both himself and all his Family, with excessive cares and labours, which is called coveting an evil covetousness to his House, Habak. 2. 9.

f Shall be as unable to keep and enjoy what he gets as a Man is to hold the VVind in his Fist, or to feed and satisfie himself with it: he shall be brought to poverty.

Ch. 17. 2.

g By which means such a troublesome fool shall through his extreme necessity be forced even to fell himself to such as are wiser.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h i. e. VVhich he produceth, his discourses and his whole conversation.

Ch. 13. 12.

i Is like the fruit of the Tree of Life, is a great preserver of this life, and a procurer of Eternal life, not onely to himself, but to others also.

Heb. taketh.

Dan. 12. 3.

k Heb. that catcheth Souls, as a Fowler doth Birds, that maketh it his design and business, and useth all his skill and diligence to gain Souls to God, and to pluck them out of the snare of the Devil.

l Sheweth himself to be a truly wise and good Man. But this Clause is and may be rendred thus, and [illegible] that is wise (the same with the Righteous in the former Clause) winneth Souls, or brings them to life. So this Clause agrees very well with the former.

entries.title: Proverbs 11:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m i. e. Punished for his sins, as appears from the next Clause, the general word being here used of this one particular, by a Synecdoche.

n VVhereby he intimates, that all his sufferings are confined to this VVorld, which is an unspeakable felicity.

o They shall be punished more certainly and more severely, either in this life, or in the next.

p Those who make sin their great study, and daily and most delightful exercise. Compare this Verse with 1 Pet. 4. 18. which is a good Conment upon it.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Admonition or reproof, as appears from the next Clause, which is a singular means of getting true and sound knowledge.

b Sheweth that he is a true lover of knowledge, because he is willing to purchase it upon such unwelcome terms, as reproofs are generally esteemed.

Ch. 15. 5.

c Discovereth himself to be a most foolish and stupid Creature, because he is an enemy to himself and to his own happiness.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. draweth out.

d Whereby he is and shall be acquitted and justified.

e Who designeth and industriously committeth wickedness.

f When he standeth in judgment, howsoever he may for the present justifie himself and deceive others into a good opinion of him.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g By any sinful courses by which he useth to secure or stablish himself; whereby he implies that he shall be rooted up.

Ch. 10. 25.

h To wit, out of its place. He shall stand fast and flourish like a welrooted Tree.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
1 Cor. 11. 7.

i A singular ornament and matter of his glorying and joy.

k That by her folly or wickedness bringeth shame to her self and to her Husband.

l Loathsom and vexatious, and pernicious.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. judgment.

m His constant purpose is to deal justly and truly with God and with men.

Ch. 11. 18.

n His great care and contrivance is to wrong and deceive others by fair pretences and cunning Artifices.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 1. 11, 38. 18.

o Are designed and ordered to intrap or deceive others, and to destroy them.

p To wit, from those that lie in wait for them: which it doth, either 1. by prayer to God for their deliverance: Or 2. by pacifying the wicked with soft and gentle answers, or by diverting them from their evil course by their good counsels and admonitions: Or 3. by pleading their righteous cause in a judicial or other way.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 37. 37. Ch. 11. 21. & 14. 11.

q Both they and their Families shall suddenly perish.

r The Family or Posterity.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
s To wit, by wise and good men.

t More or less according to the degree of Wisdom which his discourses and actions discover to be in him.

Heb. perverse of heart.

u Which he sheweth by his wicked words and conversation.

x By God and all wise men.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y That liveth in a [illegible]ean and obscure condition in the World, for such are commonly despised by men of an higher ra[illegible]k.

z Hath but one Servant. Or rather, as it is in the Margent, is Servant to himself, hath none to wait upon him or work for him but himself, that getteth Bread by his own labours.

Or, is servant to himself. So Gr.

a Is happier.

b That glorieth in his high Birth or gay attire.

c Wants necessaries for his own sustenance.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 25. 4.

Heb. knoweth. Ps. 1. 6.

d Which is employed in his Service, he will not destroy it either by labours beyond its strength, or by denying to it necessary food or rest, or by any other way: and much more will he be pitiful to his own Servants, and to poor men.

Or, bowels.

e There is much cruelty mixed even with their most merciful actions, when they pretend or intend to shew mercy. Heb. the Bowels of the, &c. those very Bowels which in others are the seat of pity in him are hardned and shut up, and onely stir him up to cruelty. In stead of that Mercy which is natural to other men, he hath nothing but cruelty. Their Mercies are here said to be cruel, as the foolishness, and weakness of God, are said to be wise and strong, 1 Cor. 1. 25.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 28. 19.

f That employeth his time and strength in an honest calling.

g That useth their society and idle course of living.

h Shall through his own folly want Bread.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, the fortress.

i He approveth and useth those cunning and deceitful arts, which wicked men use like Nets to ensnare other men, and to take their goods to themselves. Or, he desireth the Fortress of wicked men, or, of wickedness, i. e. he seeks to fortifie and stablish himself by wicked practices.

k That Justice and Piety, in which he is rooted, and which is the root of his actions, doth of it self, without the aid of any indirect and sinful courses, yield him sufficient fruit both for his own need, and to do good to others. But, because the word fruit is not in the Hebrew, and may seem to be too great a supplement, it is and may be rendred thus, the root of the Righteous giveth it, to wit, that Fortress or security which others seek in wickedness.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. the snare of the wicked is in the transgression of Lips.

Ch. 18. 7.

l i. e. Brought into trouble.

m By his wicked speeches against God and men.

n To wit, by his wise and holy, and in offensive speeches, whereby he pacifieth men and gaineth God's favour and protection.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 13. 2.

o By his pious and profitable Discourses.

p i. e. Of his works and actions, of which the hand is the great instrument. Whereby also may be implied that God will not regard nor recompence good words, unless they be accompanied with a good conversation.

q To wit, by God, to whom the work of retribution belongs.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 3. 7.

r The counsel and course which his own mind suggests to him in the ordering of his affairs.

s Highly pleaseth him, so that he neglects and despiseth the opinions and advices of others.

t That distrusteth his own judgment, and seeketh counsel from others.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. in that day.

u By his rash words and indecent actions, whereby he exposeth himself to shame.

x Either 1. the shame, or reproach, or injury done to him by others, which he concealeth and beareth with patience and passeth by, as his duty and interest obligeth him to do. Or, 2. his own shame, to which the [illegible]olly of rash anger would have betrayed him.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 13. 5. & 14. 5.

y Heb. He that will speak truth, i. e. he who accustometh himself to speak truth in common conversation; for the future Tense in the Hebrew Tongue oft notes a continued act or habit.

z To wit, as a witness in publick judgment, he will speak nothing but what is true and just; you may depend upon his Testimony.

a He who useth himself to lying in his common talk, will use falseshood and deceit in judgment.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 57. 4. & 59. 7.

b Hurtful and pernicious words, whereby they either corrupt mens minds and manners, or scandalize them, or injure them in their Reputation, Estate, or Life, or otherwise.

Or, healing. So Gr.

c His speech both in judgment, and in common discourse, is found and wholesom in it self, and tending to the comfort and benefit of others.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: d The speaker of truth is constant, and always agreeable to himself, and his words the more and longer they are tried, the more doth the truth of them appear, whereas Liars, though they may make a fair shew for a season, yet are easily and quickly convicted of falshood.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: e Either 1. towards others, whom they design to deceive, and then to destroy, whilst good Counsellers bring safety and joy to others. Or rather 2. to themselves. So the sense of the Verse is, They whose hearts devise mischief against others shall be deceived in their hopes, and bring that trouble upon themselves which they design against others; but they who by good counsels labour to promote the Peace and Happiness of others, shall reap the comfort and benefit of it to themselves.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: f Either 1. of sin, or rather 2. of suffering or mischief, as the next clause explains this: No such evil shall befall them, as doth commonly befall the wicked, who are filled, or overwhelmed, and utterly destroyed by it, whereas good men are supported under their troubles, and shall be delivered out of them, and receive much benefit by them.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 6. 17.

[illegible] do [illegible] [illegible] 3. 21.

g That speak and act sincerely and truly. He implies that although lying lips alone are sufficient to purchase Gods hatred, yet truth in a mans speech is not sufficient to procure Gods favour, unless there be also Truth and Justice in his actions.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 13. 16. [illegible] 15. 2.

h He doth not vain-gloriously and unseasonably utter what he knows, but keeps it in his breast till he hath a fit occasion to bring it forth for Gods Glory and the good of others.

i Whilest he makes ostentation of his knowledge, he betrays his Ignorance and Folly. Compare Eccles. 10. 3.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 10. 4.

k Shall procure Wealth and Power.

[illegible], deceitful.

l Heb. The deceitful. So he calls the slothful, because Deceit and [illegible]dleness are commonly companions, and such men seek to gain by Fraud what they either cannot or will not get by honest Labour. Compare Prov. 10. 4.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 15. 13.

Isa. [illegible]0. 4.

l A compassionate or encouraging word from a Friend or Minister.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible], [illegible].

m Either 1. In his temper and disposition, more just, and generous, and publick spirited, and merciful, &c. Or 2. In his condition, more happy, notwithstanding all his sufferings and the contrary opinion of the world concerning them.

n Than any other man who is unrighteous.

o That course of Life which they chuse and follow, and by which they design and expect to excel other men.

p Heb. maketh them to err or wander, to lose that excellency or happiness which they had promised to themselves, in and by their wicked practices.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q Or, The deceitful man, as v. 24. who seeks to enrich himself by fraudulent and unjust practices.

r Doth not enjoy the fruit of his Labours or devices, either because he doth not labour, and so hath nothing to waste or enjoy; or because God oft times deprives him either of such ill-gotten goods, or at least of a quiet and comfortable fruition of them.

s Yields him great comfort and satisfaction, partly because it abides with him, and partly because he hath Gods Favour and blessing with it.

entries.title: Proverbs 12:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible], [illegible].

t The practice of Justice and Godliness, though it expose a man to some dangers and inconveniences in the world, yet it will certainly lead him to Life and Happiness, whereas the end of all wicked courses is death and destruction.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Which word is understood out of the next clause, as is frequent in the Hebrew text.

b Or, Rebuke or Reproof.

c He hareth reproof either from his Father, or from any other man.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12. 14.

d Shall receive much comfort, and credit, and benefit to himself.

e By his wise and profitable discourses.

f i. e. The person, as the soul is oft used.

g Who transgress with their Lips, as this general Phrase may be restrained from the former clause.

h Shall have that violence and injury returned upon themselves which they have offered to others in word or deed.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 18. 21. & 21. 23.

i To wit, shut, for this is opposed to the opening of it: who speaks sparingly, and with due care and caution.

k Prevents many sins and mischiefs which others run into.

l That takes liberty to speak every thing which pleaseth him, or cometh into his mind

m From God or men.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 10. 4.

n Because he contenteth himself with lazy desires without diligent endeavours.

o He shall be enriched with the fruit of his own Labours.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p Both in himself and in other men, whereby he getteth that good name which is like a pretious Ointment.

q Who accustometh himself to lying, as may be gathered from the foregoing words.

Or, causeth stench & shame.

r Makes himself contemptible and hateful to all that know him; there being scarce any reproach which men more impatiently endure, and severely revenge, than that of being called or accounted a Lyar.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 11. 3, 5, 6.

s Either from [illegible]in: or from that overthrow which befals sinners in the next clause.

Heb. sin.

t Heb. the man of sin, who giveth up himself to wicked courses.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 12. 9.

u Some men who have little or nothing pretend to have great Riches, and carry themselves accordingly, either out of Pride and Vanity, or with a design to gain Reputation with others whom they intend to defraud.

x Some rich men seem and profess themselves to be very poor that they may preserve and increase their estates by concealing them from those who would either desire a share in them, or take them away by deceit or violence.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: y This verse sets forth, Either 1. The several advantages of Riches and Poverty. Riches enable a man to redeem his life when it is in greatest danger, and Poverty preserves a man from those Rebukes and Injuries which endanger and oft destroy the Rich. Or 2. The convenience of Poverty above Riches. Riches frequently expose men to the peril of losing their Lives by false Accusers, or Thieves, or Tyrants, which they are forced to redeem with the loss of their Riches; whereas Poverty commonly secures men not only from such kinds of death, but even from Rebukes and Injuries; partly because such persons are cautious, that they may not offend or provoke others; and partly because their persons and actions are neglected and slighted, and they are esteemed Objects of pity.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 22. 28.

z The Prosperity or Happiness, which is oft called a Light or Lamp in Scripture, and other Authors.

a Shineth with a pleasant and constant Brightness and Glory; for this is opposed to the putting out in the next clause. Rejoicing is here ascribed to the light, as it is to the Sun, Psal. 19. 5. both Metaphorically, because they would rejoice in it, if they were capable of any such passions, and Metonymically, because they refresh and chear mens Spirits. So Mountains and Trees are said to rejoice, Psal. 65. 12. & 96. 12.

Job 18. 6. & 21. 17.

Or, candle.

b Their felicity shall have a sudden and a dismal end.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Which is not to be understood exclusively as to all other causes; for contentions oft spring from Ignorance, or Mistake, or Covetousness, or other Passions, but eminently, because as Pride bloweth up those coals of Contention which other Lusts kindle, so oft-times Pride alone, without any other cause, stirreth up strife; which it doth by making a man self-conceited in his opinions, and obstinate in his Resolutions, and impatient of any opposition, and many other ways.

d Who are not governed by their own passions, but by prudent consideration, and the good Counsel of others.

e Which teacheth them to avoid and abhor all contention.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 10. 2. & 20. 21.

f By vain, or deceitful, or wicked practices.

g Because the Curse of God attends upon it.

Heb. with the hand.

h By diligence in an honest Calling.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i Delays in obtaining that good which a man passionately desireth and hopeth for.

k The good desired and expected, Acts being oft put for the Objects.

Ver. 19.

l It is most sweet, and satisfactory, and reviving.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n The word of God, which is called the word by way of eminency, Deut. [illegible]0. 14. Compare with Rom. 10. 18. 1 Tim. 5. 17. and elsewhere

o Except he repent, and return to his Obedience.

p That hath a Reverence to its authority, and is afraid to violate it.

Or, shall be in peace.

m Disobeyeth it wilfully and presumptuously.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 14. 27.

q The Doctrine, Instruction, or Counsel, as the word, Law, is frequently understood in Scripture.

r Of holy men, who are commonly called wise, as sinners are called Fools, in this Book.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t Discovering itself by a mans holy and righteous practices and ways, as appears from the opposition of the way of transgressors to it, and as words of Understanding in this and other Books of Scripture commonly include practice.

u Maketh a man acceptable both to God and men.

x The carriage or manner of conversation.

y Or, rough, as this very word is used, Deut. 21. 4. offensive and hateful to God and Men, as rough ways are to a Traveller, fierce, and intractable, and incorrigible.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12. 23. & 15. 2.

z Heb. Acteth, or doth, manageth all his affairs.

a Considerately and discreetly.

[illegible]eb. spreadith.

b By his heady and foolish Actions.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Who is unfaithful in the execution of that which is committed to his charge, as appears by the opposite clause.

d Shall not escape punishment from God, or from them who sent him.

e Or, wholsom, procureth safety and benefit, as to his Master, so also to himself.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Whereby he might have been kept from destructive and dishonourable courses.

g That considers it seriously, receiveth it kindly, and reformeth himself by it.

h And enriched, which is implied from the former branch. Not that it is so always, but commonly, and when God sees it good for a man. Or, if he do not always gain Riches, he shall certainly have honour both from God and men.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ver. 12.

i The satisfaction of a mans desires by the enjoyment of the things desired is very acceptable to him. Which may be taken either 1. Of the desire of Fools, which may be understood out of the next clause. So the sense of the verse is, It is sweet to sinners to indulge and satisfie their desires, which are wholly carnal and sinful, and for that reason they love sin, and hate the thoughts of leaving it, because their desires are wholly and fully set upon it. Or 2. Of good desires, or of the desires of wise and good men, as the LXX, and Chaldee, and Syriack, and Arabick Interpreters understand it, by the opposition of Fools in the next clause. So the sense may be this, The desires of good men are set upon what is good, and they rejoice when they attain to it, and are grieved when they fall short of it; but the desires of the wicked are set upon sin, and it is a pleasure to them to commit it, and an abomination to them to be hindred from it. Or rather 3. Of desires in general. Whatsoever men do earnestly desire, the enjoyment of it is very sweet and grateful to them; and therefore sinners rejoice in the pursuit and satisfaction of their sinful Lusts, and abhor all Restraint and Mortification of them: For this is certain and confessed, that many things are understood in these short proverbial Speeches which are not expressed.

k Or, and, as this particle properly signifies; or, therefore, as it is frequently used.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
l i. e. Commonly converseth and associateth himself.

m Shall learn Wisdom and Goodness both from their Counsels and Examples. The design of this Proverb is to shew the wonderful influence which a mans society hath upon him, either to save, or to corrupt and destroy him.

Heb. shall be broken.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n Evil of punishment proportionable to their evil of sin, as appears from the next clause.

o And sooner or later shall certainly overtake them, albeit they please themselves with hopes of impunity.

p Obstinate and incorrigible sinners.

q Gods blessings and true happiness.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 21. 17. & 27. 17. Chap. 28. 8. Eccl. 2. 26.

r Is by Gods powerful Providence oft-times translated to good men of another Family, who will be more faithful Stewards of it.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12. 11.

Chap. 21. 4.

s Poor and mean persons by their diligent labours in tillage or other employments, and Gods Blessing upon them oft-times grow rich.

t Or, consumed, to wit, in his estate, brought to poverty.

u Either 1. For want of discretion and convenient care and diligence in tilling his Land, and in managing his Affairs, which he neglects himself, and leaves to the care of others, whereas poor men are forced by their necessities to look to their own concerns, and to use their utmost diligence in them. Or rather 2. By Injustice, as this Phrase is used, Prov. 16. 8. Ier. 17. 11. & 22. 13. Ezek. 22. 29. Nor do I find it in any other Scripture. By his Frauds, Rapines, and Oppressions, and other unjust and wicked practices, whereby he seeks to enrich himself, as refusing and scorning to get an Estate by honest labours. So this agrees with what is said v. 11.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 19. 18. & 22. 15. & 23. 13. & 29. 1[illegible], 17.

x Heb. with-holdeth it from his Son when it is due to him.

y That correction which his Sons fault requires, and he as a Father is required to give him.

z Not directly and properly in regard of his Affection, but consequently, and in respect of the event. His fond affection is as pernicious to him as his or another mans hatred could be.

Either 1. In his tender years as soon as he is capable of it. Or 2. Speedily, before he be hardened and inveterate in sin.

entries.title: Proverbs 13:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 34. 10. & 37. 3.

Gods Favour and Blessing gives him a competent Estate, and an Heart to use it, and Comfort and Satisfaction in it, whereas wicked men commonly want either all these Blessings, or some of them.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a He speaks of the Woman not to exclude the Man, of whom this is no less true, but because the Women, especially in those times, were very industrious in managing their Husbands Estates, of which see Prov. 31.

b Maintaineth and improveth her Family and Estate, as this Phrase is used, Exod. 1. 21. 2 Sam. 7. 11. Psal. 127. 1.

c Either by her idleness and not using her hands, or by her foolish and sinful courses.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Whose conversation is sincerely pious and righteous. The design of this Proverb and Verse is to shew, that God doth, and men may judge of mens outward professions and inward dispositions by the common course of their lives.

[illegible] 12. 4.

e Plainly declares that he doth not fear God, but despise him, and his commands, and threatnings.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f His proud and insolent speeches as they are like a Rod, offensive and injurious to others, so they make a Rod for their own Backs, by provoking God and men against them. Which sense seems most probable both from the opposite Clause, and by comparing this place with Prov. 10. 13. & 26. 3. For this Phrase, The Rod of Pride, it may be compared with other like Phrases, as the foot of Pride, Psal. 36. 11. The scourge of the Tongue, Job 5. 21. and the Rod of the Mouth, Isa. 11. 4.

g From that Rod.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h The Barn or Stable is empty of food for Cattel, and much more for Man, whose food is more scarce and dear. In the same sense cleanness of Teeth is put for Famine, Amos 4. 6.
