i By their labours, or by diligence in Husbandry, which then was principally managed by Oxen.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 25. [illegible]. 20. 16. [illegible] 1. [illegible]6. 19. & [illegible] 17

k To wit, in common discourse and conversation, whereby he sheweth his love to truth, and giveth assurance that when he is called to be a Witness, he will be true and faithful.

l Or, as the words lie in the Hebrew, And, or But he that will utter lies (that accustometh himself to lying) is or will be a false Witness, when occasion requires it. Having debauched his Conscience by daily lying he is thereby prepared and disposed to false-witness-bearing. Compare Prov. 12. 17.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m A proud, self-conceited, and profane Person.

n Because he doth not seek it aright, to wit, sincerely, and earnestly, and seasonably, and in a constant and diligent use of all the means which God hath appointed to that end, and with an honest intention of employing his knowledge to the service of God, and the furtherance of his practice of Religion.

Chap. 8. 9.

o Is plain and easily attained by him.

p That knoweth and is deeply sensible of his own want of knowledge, and of the great worth and necessity of knowledge, which will make him use all possible means to it, and, among other ways, pray earnestly to God for it. Or, that is honest and pious: for words of knowledge are oft understood practically, especially in this Book.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q Avoid the company and conversation of ungodly men.

r When they break forth into foolish or wicked discourses, left thou either be infected by them, or seem to approve of them.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
s It consists not in vain Speculations, nor in a curious prying into other mens matters, nor in cunning arts of deceiving others, but in a diligent study of his own duty, and of the way to true and eternal happiness.

t The wit of ungodly men, which, though they account their Wisdom, is really their folly, is employed onely in finding out ways of over-reaching and deceiving others, and themselves too.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 10. 23.

u Wicked men, as appears from their opposition to the righteous in the next Clause.

x Please and sport themselves with their own and other mens sins, which is an high offence and provocation to God and men. Or, as others render it, excuse or cover sin, sin against God or men, and then justifie or extenuate their sins, which is to double the injury. Possibly this Clause may be thus rendred, Sin deludes or makes a mock of Fools, or sinners, i. e. exposeth them to shame and contempt, which is fitly opposed to favour in the next Clause. And thus two Ancient and Learned Interpreters, Aquila and Theodotion, render it. And this suits exactly with the Hebrew words, whereas in the other Translation the Noun and Verb governed by it are of divers Numbers, which though somtimes it be allowed, yet is not to be supposed without necessity. But this I submit to the learned and judicious.

Ch. 21. 10.

y Who are so far from making a mock of sin, or excusing it, that they do not allow themselves to commit it.

z They find favour both with God and men, as this very word thus generally expressed is used, Prov. 11. 27. because they make conscience of ordering their lives so that they offend neither God nor men, or if they offend either, they heartily repent of it, so far are they from excus[illegible]ng it or pleasing themselves with it. Or, there is good will, as the word properly and usually is taken: they have a real love, and are ready to do all Offices of kindness one to another, and therefore neither sin against others, nor rejoice in the sins of others.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. the [illegible]itterness of his Soul.

a The sense of the Verse is this, The inward griefs and joys of mens Hearts, though somtimes they may be guessed at by outward signs, yet are not certainly known to any but a mans s[illegible]lf. Compare 1 Cor. 2. 11. The scope of the Parable may be to keep men from murmuring under their own troubles or envying other mens happiness.

b Any other Person without or beside a Mans self.

c Doth not partake of it, nor understand it.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Their dwelling and family.

e Which is a weak, and poor, and unstable thing, soon reared up, and soon taken down, and is here opposed to the large, and strong, and magnificent House of wicked men.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 16. 25.

f There are some evil actions or courses which men may think to be lawful and good, either through gross and affected ignorance; or through partiality or self-flattery; or through want of necessary diligence in examining them by the rule of God's will or word; all which are culpable causes of the mistake and therefore do not excuse the error.

g The event sheweth that they were sinful and destructive.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 5. 4.

h The outward signs of joy are commonly mixed with or end in real and hearty sorrow. The design of the Proverb is to declare the vanity of all worldly joys and comforts, and to teach men moderation in them, and to persuade us to seek for more solid and durable joys.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psa. 44. 18

i He who departeth from God and from the way of his Precepts with all his Heart, which implies the doing it upon deliberation, with free choice, and full purpose, and customary practice, as ungodly men commonly do, and is opposed to the [illegible]lips of humane frailty; for otherwise every sin is a revolt from God.

Ch. 1. 31. & 12. 14.

k With the fruit of his ways or doings, the punishment of his sins.

l i. e. From his ways, as appears by the opposition from the pious temper of his own Heart which cleaveth to the Lord, when the hearts of sinners forsake him, and from the holy and righteous course of his life, from which he shall receive unspeakable comfort and satisfaction, both here and hereafter to all Eternity.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Either the harmless Man: or rather a foolish Man, because he is opposed to the prudent.

n Is easily deceived with the smooth words and fair pretences of false and deceitful men.

o Either 1. to his own going, as this is generally understood, he ordereth his conversation and dealings in the World with due circumspection, not considering so much what other men say as what he ought to do. Or, 2. to the going of the deceiver, whose the word in the former clause is suppos'd to be. So the sense is, he judgeth of mens words and professions by their conversations; which is a good rule.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch 22. 3.

p Trembleth at God's judgments when they are either inflicted or threatned.

q From sin, which is the procuring cause of all calamities.

r Fretteth against God, or is enraged against his Messengers who bring the threatning, or disquieteth himself in vain. Or transgresseth, as this Verb in its simple form and first conjugation commonly signifies, or, goeth on in sin constantly and resolutely, according to the Emphasis which this conjugation commonly adds to the simple Verb. And this is most fitly opposed to departing from evil, as being confident is opposed to fearing.

s Secure and insensible of his danger till God's judgments overtake him.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t His passion hurries him into many rash and foolish speeches and actions.

u One who suppresseth his passion, but designeth and meditateth revenge, watching for the fittest methods and opportunities of executing it.

x Both by God and men, as being most deeply malicious and like the Devil, and most dangerous and pernicious to humane Society, whereas men that are soon angry give a Man warning and are quickly pacified, and therefore pitied and pardoned.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y They possess it as their Inheritance or portion, holding it fast, improving it, delighting and glorying in it. In like manner David took God's Testimonies for his Heritage, Psal. 119. 111. where the word is the same: Withal he may imply that folly is Natural and Hereditary to them.

z They place their honour and happiness in a sound and practical, and saving knowledge of God and of their own duty, and therefore earnestly pursue after it, and Heartily embrace it.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Giving honour to them, and supplicating their favour and help, either for supply of their wants, as being brought low for their sins, or for counsel or comfort, or for their prayers to God for them.

b As Clients, and Petitioners, and Beggers use to wait at the Doors, and Houses of Great and Potent men. The sense is, Good men shall have the preeminency over the wicked, oft-times in this life, when God sees it expedient, but assuredly in the next life.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 19. 7.

c i. e. Despised and abandoned, as hateful Persons and Things are.

d Strictly so called, who is nearest to him, either by habitation or by relation, and therefore most obliged to love and help him.

Heb. many are the lovers of the Rich.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c That doth not pity and relieve the poor, as this is explained in the next Clause, the word Neighbour being here generally taken for any Man, as it is most commonly used in Scripture; which not relieving him, proceeds from a contempt of his Person.

d And therefore shall be punished for his inhumanity, which is opposed to his being happy in the next Clause.

Ps. 112. 9.

e That sheweth his compassion by his bounty and relief.

f He doth a worthy action, and shall be blessed in his deed.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g They do certainly err from the right way, and mistake their mark, and shall miss of that advantage and felicity which they promise to themselves by such practices.

h That do not onely commit it but make it their design, and study, and business, that are Artists or Masters in it, as the word signifies.

i Either 1. mischief to men. Or 2. any kind of wickedness against God or men; for the expression is general; and this seems best to agree to the following Clause.

k Either 1. from men; Men shall deal truly and kindly with them, partly because such men by their carriage oblige them to do so, and partly because God inclineth their hearts to it. Or 2. from God to whom these two properties are jointly ascribed in divers places of Scripture.

l That designedly and industriously apply themselves to the doing of all good offices to God and men.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: m Diligem labour is the ready way to riches, but idle talking, wherein too many spend most of their pretious time, will bring a Man to poverty.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n They are a singular advantage and ornament to them, partly as they make their Wisdom more regarded, when the poor Man's wisdom is despised, Eccles. 9. 16. and partly as they give a Man great opportunity to discover and exercise his Wisdom or Vertue by laying out his Riches to the honour and service of God, and to the great and manifold good of the World; which also highly tends to his own glory and happiness.

o But as for rich fools, for to them the general word is to be restrained from the opposite Clause, their folly is not cured, but made worse and more manifest by their riches. Their Riches find them Fools, and leave them Fools; they are not a Crown, but a reproach to them, and an occasion of their greater contempt. For the Phrase, we have the like in the Hebrew Text, 1 Sam. 1. 24. The Child Samuel was a Child. It is an elegant Figure called Antanaclasis used in all Authors.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Vers. 5.

p i. e Persons, to wit, such as are innocent from the mischief of false Accusations, by declaring the truth, which is sufficient for their Vindication.

q To the injury and destruction of the Innocent, which is easily understood out of the former Clause, and from the practice of false Witnesses.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r A sure ground of confidence, or a strong refuge, as the next Clause explains it.

s Either 1. God's Children. Or 2. the Children of them that fear God, who are sufficiently understood out of the former Clause.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 13. 12.

t To preserve men from deadly and destructive courses.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: u Because it is an evidence of his wise and good government. Under honour he here comprehends also strength and safety, (as appears from the opposite Clause,) which depend much upon a Princes reputation. And honour may be here put for strength, as strength is put for honour or glory, Psal. 8. 2. & 29. 1. & 96. 7.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
x Sheweth great and true wisdom in conquering his sinful and shameful passions.

Heb. short of Spirit.

y Heb. lifteth up, like a Banner, makes it known and visible to all men.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
z Free from envy and such like inordinate passions, which are commonly called the Diseases of the Soul, not onely in Sacred, but even in Heathen Writers, Or, as others render it, An healing Heart, mild, and merciful, and kind to others, which is opposed to envy.

a Procureth and maintaineth the health and vigor of the whole Body.

b It wasteth the Spirits, and consumeth even the strongest and most inward parts of the Body.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 17. 5. Mat. 25. 40, 45.

c That useth him hardly, as the Syriack renders it, that with-holdeth from him that which is his due, either by the rules of strict justice or by the great Law of Charity, of which see Prov. 3. 27. and so it is opposed to having Mercy in the next Clause.

d Whose Image the poor Man bears, which might challenge respect; Iob 31. 15. by whose counsel and providence he is made poor; 1 Sam. 2. 7. Prov. 22. 2. and who hath declared himself to be their protector and avenger.

e His Image, and Works, and Laws.

f Doth not onely forbear, oppressing or injuring of him, but affords him his pity and help.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:32
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g To wit, in his Death, as is gathered from the opposite Clause: driven away from God's favour and presence, and from the Society of the Just, and from all his hopes of Happiness both in this life and in the next. This expression notes that this is done suddenly, violently, and irresistibly, as the smoke or chaff are driven away by a strong Wind.

h Or, for his wickedness, Heb. in his evil, which may be understood of the evil of punishment; in the day of his calamity, when he shall flee to God for help.

Job 13. 15. & 19. 26. Ps. 23. 4. 1 Cor. 15. 19. 2 Cor. 1. 9.

i Of deliverance from it, or of great and everlasting advantage by it.

k In his greatest dangers and distresses, yea even in I eath it self, which therefore he can receive with comfort and confidence.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:33
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 12. 23.

l Is laid up and hid there, and not vainly nor rashly uttered by him, but only upon necessary or fit occasions.

m i. e. In the heart, which is expressed by this very word, Psal. 64. 6. and elsewhere. That Folly which is there instead of Wisdom: or, that small degree of Wisdom or Knowledg which they have.

r They will publish it in all times and companies, without any consideration or discretion.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:34
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o Maketh it honourable in the Eyes of God, and of all other Nations, as it did the ancient Romans.

[illegible]

p Brings contempt and ruine upon them by provoking both God and men against them.

entries.title: Proverbs 14:35
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 17. 2.

q Both to himself, by his foolish management of the Kings affairs commited to him, and to the King who made so foolish a choice of a Servant.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] [illegible]. 15.

a Mild or gentle.

b Which may imply a foregoing charge or accusation, although the word is and may be rendred, speech or discourse.

c From the speaker.

d Fierce and vexatious Replies or Speeches.

e Kindle it, and cause it to flame forth.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Expressing what he knows prudently and gracefully, taking due care both what, and when, and to whom, and in what manner he speaks.

[illegible] [illegible]. [illegible] 12. 23. [illegible]. 16.

[illegible]

g Plentifully, continually, promiscuously, and vehemently as a Fountain doth Waters, as this word signifies.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 3[illegible]. 21. [illegible] 5 21. [illegible]. 16. 17. [illegible]. 1[illegible]. [illegible] 13.

h His Knowledg and Providence.

i Who are first mentioned because they either doubt of, or deny Gods Providence.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]

k Which [illegible]ereth sound, and comfortable, and useful Counsels.

l Is greatly useful to preserve the present Life, and to promote the Spiritual and Eternal Life, both of the Speaker and Hearers.

m All sorts of false or corrupt Speeches.

n Disturbs and wounds, and oft-times corrupts and destroys the Spirits or Souls both of the Speaker and Hearers.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 10. 1. [illegible] 18. [illegible]. 21. 32.

o Doth not regard nor obey it, which is an evidence of contempt.

p Who hath both Love to him, and Authority over him; which greatly aggravates his Folly.

q The reproof of any person whatsoever, and much more of a Father.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r Or, Family. Whereby he implies that it is not only enjoyed by him, but also left to his posterity.

s Though he may obtain great revenues, yet they are attended with much trouble & vexation, either because they are strangely blasted and taken from them, or because they are imbittered to them by their own insatiable desires, or tormenting cares and fears, or the horrours of their guilty Consciences, or by divers other ways.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t Freely communicate to others what they know, as they have opportunity.

u Either because he hath no knowledg to disperse, or because he hath not an heart to perform his duty, or to do good to others. Or, as others render it, and as the last Hebrew word is rendred, Gen. 42. 34. and elsewhere, is not right; or, the place may be rendred, the heart of foolish (understand out of the former clause, as is very usual, disperseth by his Lips) that which is not right, foolish and corrupt discourse, which is fitly opposed to knowledg.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible].

x All the religious services, yea, the best and most costly of them; one kind being put for all the rest.

y The cheapest and meanest services.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
z The Conversation or Course of Life. This verse seems to contain a reason of the foregoing. God hates wicked mens religious Performances, because they are accompanied with ungodly Lives, and they pull down with one hand what they build with another.

a That earnestly desires, and constantly and diligently endeavours to be holy and righteous in the course of his Life, although he doth not attain to that perfect Righteousness which he thirsts after.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, instruction.

b He hateth Reproof, because it is a reproach to him, and because it strikes at that sin which he loveth.

c Gods way, emphatically called the way here, as also Psal. 119. 1. & 139. 24. Prov. 2. 13.

d i. e. Be destroyed, both here and for ever: which is a more grievous thing than an harsh reproof.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 26. 6.

e Put for the place of destruction, by an usual Metonymy, the place and state of the damned, of which men know nothing but by divine Revelation.

2 Chr. [illegible]. [illegible]0. Psal. 7. 9. & 44. 21. Joh. 2. 24, 25. & 21. 17. Acts 1. 24.

f Whose thoughts and affections, though they lie deep, discover themselves by outward signs and actions.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g i. e. Hateth and avoideth it; for more is here understood than is expressed, as it is Prov. 11. 21. & 12. 3. and elsewhere.

h Seek their Company and Conversation, as his duty and interest obligeth him.

i i. e. The godly, because he knows they who are so indeed will make Conscience of reproving him.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 17. 22.

k Either 1. His vital Spirits. Or rather 2. His Courage and Vigor, the decay whereof sheweth it self in his Countenance, as is implied from the former clause.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: l Their hearts are set upon wickedness, which is meat and drink to them.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Of the troubled in mind or heart, as this general Expression may very fitly be restrained from the following clause.

n Tedious and uncomfortable, he takes no content in any time or thing.

o Heb. of a good heart, i. e. composed, and quiet, and contented.

p Hath constant satisfaction and delight in all conditions, yea, even in affliction.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 37. 16. Chap. 16. 8. 1 Tim. 6. 6.

q Which gives a man Tranquillity and Comfort in what he hath.

r Tumultuous Lusts and Passions, Vexations Cares, and Fears, Horrours of Conscience, and expectation of Gods Curse and Judgment, which Riches gotten without Gods Fear do commonly produce.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 17. 1.

s True Friendship and Kindness between those that eat together.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 26. 21. & 29. 22.

t Because he is very apt both to give, and to take all occasions of contention.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u The way in which he doth or ought to walk, any good work which he pretends or desires to undertake.

x As a way hedged up with Thorns, as it is expressed, Hos. 2. 6. troublesom, and perplexed, and full of such difficulties as he despaireth, and therefore never striveth to overcome.

y Who is always diligent in his Calling, which is one branch of Righteousness, and therefore is fitly opposed to the slothful, who is joined with the wicked, Mat. 25. 26. and censured as such both in Scripture and Heathen Authors, because idleness is both in itself a sin, and it leads the way to many other wickednesses.

Heb. is raised up as a causey.

z Is easie and pleasant to him, notwithstanding all his discouragements and difficulties.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a By giving him that Honour and Obedience which he oweth to him.

b Whereby he maketh her sad. See the notes on Prov. 10. 1. where we have the same Proverb.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 10. 23.

c He doth not only work Wickedness, but taketh pleasure in it.

Heb. [illegible] of heart.

d Heb directeth, or maketh streight his going, i. e. ordereth all his actions by the rule of Gods word, and delighteth in so doing, which is understood from the opposite clause.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 11. 14. & 20 [illegible]8.

e When men do not seek, or will not receive advice from others in weighty affairs.

f Their designs are ill managed, and succeed accordingly.

g i. e. Of wise and good Counsellors, for such only deserve that name.

h i. e. Accomplished and brought to a good issue.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i i. e. By a wise, or good and seasonable Answer or Advice, as is manifest both from the opposite clause, and from the nature of the thing, because it is manifest and undeniable, that a foolish Answer can be no credit nor comfort to the Answerer. Thus above v. 10. the way is put for Gods way; and such Synecdoche's are frequent in Scripture.

Heb. in his season.

k Counsel or comfort given to another in fit time and manner.

l It is highly acceptable and useful.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Phi. 3. 20. Col. 3. 1, 2.

m The way or course which a wise man taketh to preserve and obtain Life, is to place his Heart, and Treasure, and Conversation in things above, and to manage all his affairs in this world with due respect and subserviency to the happiness of a better Life.

n Or, from the lowermost hell, not from the grave, as this word is elsewhere used, for no wisdom can prevent that, but from hell properly so called, as this word is elsewhere used, as hath been formerly observed.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 12. 7. & 14. 11.

o Of the most mighty Oppressors, who conceit themselves to be unmoveably fixed.

Psal. 68. 5, 6.

p Either 1. The Estate, the border being oft used for the Land within the Borders, as Psal. 105. 31, 33. and elsewhere. Or 2. The Border by which Lands were then bounded and distinguished, which those proud persons endeavoured to remove contrary to Gods Law, Deut. 19. 14. & 27. 17.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 6. 18.

q And much more their words which express their thoughts; for thoughts are said to be free, and wicked men are seldom, and but little concerned for the sins of their thoughts.

r Which discover and proceed from their thoughts, Mat. 15. 19.

Heb. words of pleasantness.

s acceptable to God, which is opposed to abomination to him.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 1. 19.

t That seeketh wealth by unjust courses, as appears from the opposite clause

u Bringeth Gods Curse and Destruction upon himself and his Family, whom he designed to enrich and establish.

x Who refuseth them not with dissimulation, nor only from prudential Reasons, but from an hearty abhorrency of all Unrighteousness.

y i. e. Bribes given to corrupt Judgment. See Exod. 18. 21. & 23. 8. Deut. 16. 19.

z Shall preserve himself and (which is understood out of the former clause) his Family from ruine.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 16. 23.

a He answers or speaks considerately and conscientiously, and therefore profitably, or to the use and Edification of the Hearers.

b Not the Heart, for he is without Heart in Scripture account, and he rashly speaks what comes into his mouth, without the direction of his Heart or Conscience.

c Foolish, and unprofitable, and hurtful Speeches.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 34. 1[illegible].

d To wit, when they pray to him, as the next clause explains, and therefore doth not hear nor regard them, as he is said to be nigh to the righteous, Psal. 34. 18. & 145. 18. But this farness or nearness respecteth not Gods Essence, which is every where, but his gracious and helpful presence.

Psal. 145. 18, 19.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e The light which we see with our Eyes, and by the help of which we see many other pleasant Objects is a great comfort and refreshment. Compare Eccles. 11. 7. Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the Sun: which is a good Comment upon this place.

Or, goodness as Ch. 25. 25.

f Either 1. Glad tidings. Or rather 2. A Good-Name, which is a more lasting thing, and makes deeper impression.

g Not only cheareth a man for the present, but gives him such solid and stable comfort as doth both revive his soul, and give Health and Vigour to his body. So he compares two Senses together, Seeing and Hearing, with respect to their several Objects, and prefers the latter before the former.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h The man that hearkeneth to it, and delights in it.

i That Reproof and good Counsel which leads to Life.

Ver. 5. & Chap. 12. 1.

k Heb. shall or will abide, &c. Either 1. He will thereby be made wise, and be esteemed one of that number. Or rather 2. He seeketh and delighteth in the Company and Conversation of the Wise, by whom he may be admonished, as on the contrary, Fools who hate Reproof do avoid and abhor the Society of Wise men and Reprovers, Amos 5. 10.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:32
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, correction.

l Which hereby he exposeth to the danger of utter destruction, whereby he shews his Folly.

Or, obeyeth.

Heb. possesset an heart.

m Whereby he saveth his Soul. Heb. possesseth an heart, which the Hebrews make the seat of Wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs 15:33
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n Doth instruct men in, or lead them to true Wisdom; whence it is said to be the beginning of Wisdom, Prov. 1. 7. & [illegible]. 10.

Chap. 18. 12

o i. e. It is the ready way to Honour both from God, and from Men.

p Whereby men submit to God, and yield to Men, which gains them Love and Respect, whereas Pride procures them Hatred and Contempt from God and Men.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ver. 9. & Ch. 19. 2[illegible] & 20. 24. Jer. 10. 23.

Or, dis[illegible]

a Men can neither think nor speak wisely and well of themselves, or without divine assistance. Or, as many others, both ancient and modern Interpreters render the verse, The preparations, or dispositions, or orderings of the heart are in or from a man, (i. e. a man may consider and contrive in his own thoughts what he wills or designs to speak. Which is spoken by way of concession, yet not excluding mans dependance upon God therein, which is evident both from many plain Texts of Scripture, and from undeniable Reason.) but the answer or speech (as this word is oft used) of the tongue is from the Lord. Men cannot express their own thoughts without Gods leave and help, and their tongues are oft over-ruled by God to speak what was besides and above their own thoughts, as he did Balaam, Numb. 23. and Cajaphas, Ioh. 11. 49, 50, 51.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. [illegible]1

b Many Men can easily flatter and deceive themselves into a good opinion of themselves, and of their own actions, though they be sinful. See below, v. 25. and compare 1 Cor. 4. 4.

c i. e. Exactly knoweth, as men do the things which they weigh and examine.

d The hearts of men, from which both mens actions, and the goodness and badness of them in a great measure, proceeds, their ends and intentions, their dispositions and affections, which are hid not onely from others, but oft times from a mans self; whereby he is unfit to judge in his own cause, and easily mistaken, if he do not use great diligence and fidelity. In this last clause he intimates the reason why men deceive themselves, in judging of their state and Actions, because they do not search their own hearts.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 37. 5. [illegible] 55. 22. Mat. 6. 25. Luke 12. 22 [illegible]. 5. 7.

Heb. roll.

e Heb. roll, &c. as a man rolls a burden to another, which is too heavy for himself, imploring his help. Refer all thy actions and concerns to God, and to his Glory, as the end of them, and in the discharge of thy own duty depend upon Gods Providence for assistance and success.

f Thy honest desires and designs shall be brought to an happy issue one way or other.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Or, hath wrought, or doth work; for the Hebrews express the present as well as the past time by this tense: he ordereth or disposeth: for this may be understood either of the works of Creation, or of Providence.

h And especially all men

i For his own service and glory, for the discovery and illustration of his own Wisdom, Power, Goodness, Truth, Justice, and his other most glorious Perfections.

[illegible]ob 21. 20. [illegible]. 9. 22.

k Wilful and impenitent Sinners.

l For the time of punishment, as this Phrase is used, Psal. 49. 5. Ier. 17. 18. and elsewhere: of which the Scripture frequently speaks, both to warn sinners of their danger, and to satisfie the minds of them which are amazed and disquieted with the consideration of the present impunity and felicity of wicked men. Men make themselves wicked, and God therefore makes them miserable.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 6. 17. [illegible] 13.

m Though he dissemble it in his outward carriage and countenance, as Psal. 10. 4. In whose heart Pride rules.

n Though they have many Friends and Assistants. See the same Phrase, Prov. 11. 21.

[illegible].

entries.title: Proverbs 16:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o Either 1. By Gods Mercy or Grace, and by his truth in performing his Promises made to sinners in Christ. Or 2 By mens Mercy and Truth, as those very words are jointly used, Prov. 3. 3. & 20, 28. and elsewhere; and as, in the following clause, the fear of the Lord is a Grace or Disposition in men: by a merciful and just and faithful frame of heart and course of Life: which are here opposed to Sacrifices, as mercy is, Hos. 6. 6. by which the hypocritical Jews expected to obtain the expiation of their sins.

[illegible].

p Not meritoriously but instrumentally, as they qualifie a man to offer up acceptable Prayers to God for the Pardon of his sins, and to receive and apply to himself that pardon which Christ by his Blood hath purchased for all sincere Believers, who are filled with Mercy and Truth, and other Graces.

q By a filial Reverence or Respect unto God, and by an holy fear of offending God, and by a dread of Gods judgments.

r They are kept from abusing pardoning Mercy, and from returning to Folly or Wickedness. So he sheweth that Justification and Sanctification are constant and inseparable Companions.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: s By disposing their hearts to kindness towards him.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 37. 16.

t This was in effect said before, Prov. 15. 16. and is here repeated, partly because of the great importance and usefulness of this truth, and partly because men are very hardly brought to a serious belief of it.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ver. 1.

u Considers and proposeth to himself what he will do.

x Overruleth and disposeth all their designs and actions as he pleaseth, and not as they list.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. divi [illegible].

y Heb. Divination, which is somtimes taken in a good sense for Prudence, as it is, Isa. 3. 2. A great sagacity and piercing judgment to discern dubious and difficult cases.

z Or, should be, for the verb is wanting in the Hebrew, and this may be supplied as well as is. And he seems not so much to speak of the matter of Fact, as if it were thus in all Kings, which is notoriously and confessedly untrue, as of the duty of Kings, in whom Wisdom is a necessary qualification. For thus the two following Proverbs concerning Kings, v. 12. 13. must be understood, otherwise they are repugnant to common Experience.

a Either 1. Of wise Kings, who onely are worthy of that Name and Office; King being here put for a wise King, as a Name is put for a good Name, and a Woman for a good Woman, Eccles. 7. 28. and then this is true in fact, as it was in David, 2 Sam. 14. 17. and in Solomon, 1 Kin. 3. 28. Or 2. Of Kings in general, in the sense before given: for seeing the word is generally expressed without any limitation both here and v 12, 13. it may seem presumption to confine it to those few Kings which are, or were, wise and good.

Chap. 20. 8.

b Or, Shall, or should not transgress, or go beyond the bounds of Religion and Justice.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Lev. 19. 36. Chap. 11. 1.

c Are Gods work, as it follows, made by his direction and appointment, so as no man can corrupt or alter them without violating Gods Rights and Authority, and incurring his displeasure.

Heb. all the stones.

d Heb. the stones, which they then used as weights. See on Prov. 11. 1.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e They should not onely abstain from all wicked practices, but abhor them both in their own persons, and in all their servants and subjects. It is too plain, that he speaks not of the common practice, but of the duty, of Kings, as on v. 10. And such affirmative expressions are oft used in Scripture to express mens duty onely, as 1 Cor. 6. 19. your body is (i. e. should be) the temple, &c. and 7. 32. careth, &c. i. e. ought to care.

Ch. 20. 28. & 25. 5. & 29. 14.

f And (which is implied) weakned, and sometimes overthrown by unrighteousness; and therefore this is necessary for their own security and happiness.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: g All wise and good Kings do, and all Kings should, delight in employing such Counsellors, Judges, and Officers under them, as are just and faithful in their Counsels, and Sentences, and Actions, because such bring great honour and advantage to them.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 19. 12

h Is as terrible as if many Messengers were sent to denounce the sentence of death, and to execute it.

i Will use all prudent and lawful means to pacifie it.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k His Favour and smiling Countenance is most sweet and refreshing, especially to him that was under a Sentence of death, v. 14.

Ch. 19. 12.

l As acceptable as those clouds which brings the latter Rain, whereby the fruits are filled and ripened a little before the Harvest: of which see Deut. 11. 14. Iob 29. 23. Iam. 5. 7.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 8. 11, 19.

m It is inexpressibly and unconceivably better, as this Phrase implies, Psal. 31. 19. & 36. 7. & 92. 5. &c.

n Because it brings a man more certain, and compleat, and lasting comfort and advantage.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o Their common road, in which they constantly purpose and desire, and customarily use, to walk, although somtimes through frailty or temptation they slip into the by-paths of sin.

p From the evil of sin, and consequently from the evil of punishment.

q That takes heed to walk in that high-way.

r From that mischief which befalls those that walk in the crooked paths of wickedness.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 11. 2. & 18. 12.

s It is commonly a forerunner and cause of mens ruine, because it highly provokes both God and Men.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: t Who will spoil and rob others to maintain their own Pomp and Luxury.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, he that understandeth a matter.

u He who orders his affairs with discretion. Or, as others, both ancient and later Interpreters take it, He that understandeth, or at endeth to the Word. to wit, the Word of God, which is called absolutely the Word, Prov. 13. 13. and elsewhere, making that the rule of his actions.

x Shall obtain happy success.

Psal. 2. 12. & 34. 8. & 125. 1. Isa. 30. 18. Jer. 17. 7.

y Who doth not trust to his own prudence or diligence, but to God's providence and blessings. Or, who mixeth God's Word with Faith, as the Phrase is, Heb 4. 2.

z He shall not onely find some good, but shall certainly attain to true happiness.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a The sense is either, 1. He who hath Wisdom or sound knowledg in his Heart, will shew it by his prudence in [illegible] his Actions. Or rather, 2. He who is truly wise, or prudent, or intelligent (all which words most commonly signify one and the same thing, both in this and in other Books of Scripture) shall be so called or accounted by others.

b Eloquence added to Wisdom, the faculty of expressing a Man's mind fitly, and freely, and acceptably.

c Both in himself, for whilst a Man teacheth others, he improveth himself; and especially in others, who by this means are induced to hear and receive his good instructions. Wisdom gets a Man repute with others, but this faculty of right speaking, makes a wise Man more instrumental to do good to others.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 13. 14. & 14. 27.

d Is conti[illegible]ually suggesting wholesom and saving Instructions

e And to others also, as is understood from the following clause.

f Their most grave and serious counsels are foolish.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. maketh wise.

g Directeth him what, and when, and how to speak, and keepeth him from speaking rashly and foolishly.

h i. e. Inableth him to speak learnedly and wisely. Or, increaseth Learning (in himself and others) by (as this Hebrew Particle oft signifies, and is by some rendred here) his lips, i. e. by his wise speeches; that this may agree with the latter clause of v. 21. where this same Phrase is used.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 15. 26.

i The Discourses of the wise, last mentioned, v. 23. which yield both profit and delight, their wholesom counsels and refreshing comforts.

k To the body, Synecdochically expressed by the Bones, the strongest and greatest parts of it, and the supporters of the rest.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: l This whole Verse was delivered before Ch. 14. 12. and is here repeated partly for its great importance and usefulness to prevent that self-deceit, which is so common and dangerous: and partly to keep men from leaning too much to their own understanding, and to oblige them to seek and receive the good counsels of wise and holy men.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Eccles. 6. 7.

Heb. the Soul of him that laboureth.

m For his own use and benefit. The scope of the Proverb is to commend and press diligence in a Man's calling, and to condemn idleness.

Heb. boweth unto him.

n Heb. boweth to him, as a suppliant, beggeth him to labour that it may have somthing to put into it for its own comfort, and for the nourishment of the whole Body.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. a man of Belial.

o Inventeth or designeth mischief to others and prosecuteth his evil designs with great and constant industry.

p As his thoughts, so also his words are very vexatious and pernicious; his Tongue is set on fire of Hell, and sets himself and others on fire by lyes and slanders, and other provoking speeches.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 6. 14. 19. & 15. 18. & 26. 21. & 29. 22.

q Or, perverse, who perverteth his words and ways, who pleaseth not God, and is contrary to men, as was said of the Jews, 1 Thess. 2. 15.

r by whispering such things as may provoke one against another.

Ch. 17. 9.

s Who secretly carry Tales from one to another, publishing those evil words and actions which they should conceal, and detracting from their good actions, and perverting such as are innocent with their false constructions.

t Heb. a chief Friend, the Singular number put for the Plural, as is frequent in the Hebrew Text.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u Heb. A Man of violence, i. e. devoted to violent and injurious, courses.

x Into a confederacy with him in his wicked practices, as it follows.

y i. e. That is very sinful, as this Phrase is used, Prov 17. 26. & 18. 5. and oft elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. s[illegible] eth [illegible].

z That his Thoughts may be more free and intent to contrive mischief.

a Which is the gesture, either 1. of one whose Thoughts are deeply engaged. Or 2. of one that speaketh or maketh signs to others to assist him in executing that wickedness which he hath contrived.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 20. 29.

b A great Honour and Ornament, as it is a singular Blessing of God, a token of great experience and prudence, as it comes nearest to God, who is called, The Ancient of Days, Dan. 7. 9.

Heb i[illegible] [illegible] or, [illegible] be found.

c If it be accompanied with true Piety, otherwise an old Sinner is accu[illegible]sed, Isa. 65. 20. Heb. it shall be found, &c. This is a priviledge promised to righteous Persons, Exod. 20. 12. Prov. 3. 16. & 4. 22. whereas ungodly men shall not live out half their days, Psal. 55. 23.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:32
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Not apt to revenge, but ready to forgive, injuries.

e Because he is more like to God, more wise to foresee and to prevent mischief both to himself and others, which oft cometh from rash anger, of a more gallant and generous spirit, and more valiant and victorious, as i[illegible] follows. This is opposed to the perverse judgment of the World, who esteem such Persons pusillanimous and cowardly.

f That subdueth his passions; for his victory is the more glorious, because he fights with the stronger enemy, he conquers by his own, and not by other, mens hands and he gets a greater glory and advantage to himself and that without the injury and ruine of others, wherewith the Conquests of Cities are commonly attended.

entries.title: Proverbs 16:33
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 18. 18.

g As the ancient practice was in dividing Inheritances, and deciding doubtful things, of which see Numb. 26. 55. Ios. 7. 16. 1 Sam. 10. 20 21. & 14. 41, 42. Prov. 1. 14. Act. [illegible]. 26.

Heb. judgment.

h The event though casual to men, is directed and determined by God's counsel and providence.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 15. 17.

Or, good c[illegible]ear.

a Of the remainders of Sacrifices, of which they used to make Feasts: of which see on Prov. 7. 14. Or, of slain Beasts, as that word is used, Gen. 31. 54. and elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
b Either as being by his Father appointed Tutor or Guardian to his Son; or being by his Wisdom advanced to that Estate and Dignity, which the other possibly hath lost by his folly.

c Partly as a just recompence for his faithful Service, as Gen. 15. 2, 3, &c. and partly as an Obligation to him, to take care of his Children.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 26. 2. Ch. 27. 21. Jer. 17. 10. Mal. 3. 3.

The trial of.

The trial of.

d The Hearts of men cannot be searched and known by any humane art, but by God onely.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e Or, a malicious or mischievous Man, whose practice and delight it is to bring trouble to others.

Heb. lips of Iniquity.

f Heb. to Lips of Iniquity, to any wicked counsels or speeches, to false Accusations and Calumnies, which give him occasion and encouragement to do mischief.

g He who accustometh himself to false and wicked speaking delighteth in the like speeches of other men. This Proverb contains a comparison between an evil-doer, and an evil speaker, and sheweth their agreement in the same sinful practice of being greedy to hear false and wicked speeches.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 14. 31

h Derideth or reproacheth him with or for his poverty.

i God who by his Providence made him poor. See the same assertion, Prov. 14. 31.

k At the miseries of other men.

Heb. held innocent.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 127. 3, 1[illegible]8. 3.

l Their honour and [illegible]appiness, because they are in themselves Blessings of God and Testimonies of God's favour, although sometimes they may become the shame of their Fathers House.

m Namely such Fathers as are wise and godly, as is evident from the nature of the thing, for wicked Parents bring infamy upon their Children.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. a lip of [illegible].

n Either 1. discourse of high and excellent things far above his capacity. Or, 2. lofty or eloquent speech, which fools oft affect. Or 3. vertuous and godly Discourse.

o Either properly so called: Or, as this word is most commonly used in this Book, a wicked man, whose actions give the lye to his Expressions.

[illegible].

entries.title: Proverbs 17:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 18. 16.

[illegible]. a stone [illegible].

p Pleasant and acceptable, and withal dazleth his eyes.

q Heb. of the Lord, or owner of it, either 1. of the giver: Or rather 2. of the Receiver of it, who by the giver is made Lord of it, for to his eyes it was exposed, that he might discern the beauty and worth of it and thereby be allured to do what was desired, which accordingly he did, as it here follows.

r To whomsoever it is presented But this, as also many other Proverbs, are to be understood of the common course or effect with most men, but not universally of all men.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 10. 12.

s That concealeth, as far as he may, other mens faults against himself or against their friends.

[illegible].

t i. e. Findeth or obtaineth, as this word is used here below, v. 19. & Prov. 11. 27.

u Either 1. to himself. Or rather 2. to the transgressor, or offending friend; he maintains love among Friends, as it may be explained from the opposite clause.

y Or, the matter last mentioned, to wit, the transgression.

z Either 1. he alienateth his Friend from himself. Or rather 2. he raiseth jealousies and dissensions among Friends. This Phrase we had before, Ch. 16. 28.

x That publisheth and spreadeth it abroad, that recals it to mind after it was past and forgotten.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible], a reproof [illegible] more a [illegible] [illegible], than [illegible] [illegible] a fool [illegible] [illegible] [illegible].

a Is more effectual for his reformation.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
b It is the constant study and business of wicked men to rebel, either 1. against men in Authority. But this is not universally true, for many most wicked Persons are not guilty of that sin. Or rather 2. against God: For 1. thus it is true of all wicked men. 2. This word is used of rebellion against God, Deut. 31. 27. Ezek. 2. 5, 6. & 3. 9, &c. 3. This word being put alone without any addition of the object seems most probably to be meant of the highest and worst kind of rebellion, according to the common rule of interpretation in such cases.

c Or, a cruel Angel, the Angel of Death, the Devil, or some bloody men employed by God to avenge his quarrel; or some dreadful punishment; it being very usual in Scripture to represent things under the notion of Persons, as Rom. 7. and elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 13. 8.

d When she is most cruel and fierce.

e In the heat of his lust or passion, because the danger is greater., all things considered, and more unavoidable.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 12. 17. [illegible]. 5. 15. 1 [illegible]. 3. 9.

f From his Person and Family; because such a Man is most hateful to God and to all Mankind, God will punish him, and men will not pity nor relieve him.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g By cutting the Bank of a River, in which case the Water quickly widens the breach and breaks in with irresistible violence and fury, and causeth great mischief and destruction.

[illegible]. 20. 3.

h Avoid the occasions, and prevent the beginnings of contention.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] [illegible] Ch. [illegible] [illegible]4. Isa. 5. 23

i That acquitteth him as innocent by a judicial Sentence, or otherwise approveth or commendeth his evil practices. By which we may easily understand what it is to condemn the just.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k The Question implies that it is unworthily placed and that it is to no purpose or benefit of the Possessor.

l Possessions or Riches as all the ancient Translators render it, of which this word is used, Isa. 55. 1. and elsewhere, under which all opportunities and abilities of getting it are comprehended.

m [illegible]or the obtaining whereof, rich Men have many and great advantages above others.

n Neither common discretion to discern the worth of Wisdom, and his advantage to get it, nor any sincere desire to get it; for the heart is commonly used in Scripture both for the understanding, and for the will and affections.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 18. 24.

o A sincere and hearty Friend.

p Not onely in prosperity, but also in adversity, when false Friends forsake us.

q Who is so not onely by Name and Blood, but by brotherly affection.

r Was sent into the World for this among other ends, that he might comfort and relieve his Brother in his adversity. So this Proverb compareth a Friend with a Brotherand sheweth that a Friend doth that freely, and by choice, which a Brother doth by the force and obligations of Nature. But this last clause may be, and is by divers otherwise rendred, and he (to wit, the Friend) is Born a Brother (or, becomes, or is made a Brother, i. e. puts on brotherly affection, as if he had received a second Birth and was born his Brother, such expressions being not unusual both in Scripture, and in other Authors) in or against the time of adversity. So the sense is, He is a Friend at all Times, but in adversity he is more than an ordinary Friend, even a Brother.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 6. 1. & 11. 15.

Heb. heart.

s In token of his becoming Surety: of which Phrase, and of the thing it self, see on Prov. 6. 1. & 11. 15.

t The Friend here is either 1. before, and to the Creditor. Or rather 2. before, and with, and for the Debtor, for whom, as being his Friend, he becomes Surety, as the manner of Friends is. See on Prov. 6. 3. And this Proverb is fitly placed after that v. 17. to intimate, that although the laws of Friendship oblige us to love and help our friends in trouble, as far as we are able, yet they do not oblige us to become Surety for them rashly, and above what we are able to pay, for by that means we make our selves unable to do good either to them, or to others, or to our selves.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u Because contention is in it self a sin, and is commonly accompanied or followed with many sins, as detraction, malice, hatred, pride, &c.

Or. house. Gen. 28. 17.

x Either 1. his mouth. i. e. who speaketh loftily: for we read of the gate or door of ones Mouth in Mich. 7. 5. and elsewere: but then the word Mouth or Tongue is added to determine the sense: but the Mouth is nowhere called the gate, simply or absolutely Or 2. the Gate of his House, that maketh it, and consequently his House, lofty and Magnificent, beyond what befits his quality. which being an evidence and effect of pride and haughtiness of Spirit is here mentioned for all the rest. So the sense is, He who carries himself loftily and scornfully.

y He seeks those things which will expose him to destruction, because he maketh himself odious both to God and men. Or findeth destruction; seeking being put for finding or procuring as above v. 9.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. the froward of Heart.

z Whose Heart is not plain and upright, but false towards God or men.

a Shall not get that advantage by his dissimulation which he intends and expects, but shall fall into mischief, as is implied from the opposite Clause.

b That speaks deceitfully or wickedly So here is a comparison between an evil heart and an evil Tongue, and the ill effects of both of them.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Not a Natural, but a wilful fool, or a wicked Son.

* Ch. 10. 1[illegible]

d And consequently the Mother also.

e Which Parents usually have in the Birth of a Child, and especially of a son, but hath great cause of sorrow the contrary being implied in this and such like expressions, as in Scripture, as Prov. 10. 2, &c. so also in profane Authors: whose words see in my Latin Synopsis.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Chearfulness of Soul, especially that which is solid, and ariseth from the witness of a good Conscience.

g Even to the Body, it contributes very much to the restoration or preservation of bodily Health and Vigour, as Physicians observe, and Experience sheweth.

Or, to a medicine.

* Ch. 15. 13. & 12. 25.

h Sad and dejected

i Wasteth the marrow of the Bones, and the moisture and strength of the Body.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k Whether Judge or Witness.

l In secret, as this Phrase is expounded, Prov. 21. 14. being privily conveyed from the bosom of the giver into his own bosom.

m To give or procure an unjust sentence.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Eccles. 2. 14. & 8. 1.

n Or, in (as the particle peth is used, Deut. 2. 7. and is here rendred by divers Interpreters) the face or countenance. The sense is either 1. His Wisdom appears even in his gestures and looks, which are modest, and composed, and grave. Or 2. Wisdom is before him, or in his sight, as the mark at which he aims, or as the rule by which he constantly walketh, and ordereth all his steps, from time to time minding his present duty and business.

o The sense of this clause also is either 1. His folly appears in his light, and unsteddy, and disorderly carriage and looks. Or 2. His mind is wavering and unsettled, he neither proposeth a right and certain end to himself, nor is he constant in the use of fit means to attain it, he neglects his present business, and true interest, and wanders hither and thither in the pursuit of earthly vanities, minding most those things which are remotest from him, and least concern him.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 10. 1. & 15. 20. & 19. 13.

p This he said before, Prov. 15. 20. and elsewhere, but he here repeats it as a point of great moment and constant use, and as a powerful motive to oblige both Children to carry themselves wisely and dutifully to their Parents, as they would not be thought to be unnatural or inhumane, and Parents to educate their Children prudently and religiously, at least for their own comfort, if not for the publick good.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q This particle seems to have relation to the next foregoing Proverb to imply that it is a very evil thing for Children to cause grief to their Parents, as it is also to do what here follows.

Heb. to mulct or fine.

r For Parents, or Princes, or Rulers, to whom alone this power belongs, to punish innocent and good men.

s is highly evil and abominable, as is implied. See above, v. 20. and Prov. 16. 29. & 17. 10. &c.

t Nor to smite Magistrates, either with the Hand or Tongue, for the execution of Justice, as condemned persons are apt to do. Or, as some learned Interpreters render it, Nor for Princes to strike any man for equity or for doing his duty, or what is just. So this clause best agrees with the former. Besides it belongs to Princes or Magistrates to punish or strike.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Jam. 1. 19.

u Heb. restraineth, as at other times, so especially when he is provoked to passion, in which case fools utter all their mind.

Or, a cool spirit.

x Which he sheweth by commanding his passions, and bridling himself from hasty and unadvised speeches. Or, as others render it, is of a cool Spirit, calm and moderate, not easily provoked, humble, as the Chaldee renders it, patient or long-suffering, as the LXX and Arabick Interpreters render the words. Or, as others, sparing (Heb. precious, which is put for rare or scarce, 1 Sam. 3. 1. Prov. 25. 17. Isa. 13. 12.) of his breath, i. e. of his speech, as this very word is used, Prov. 29. 11. Isa. 11. 4. compared with 2 Thes. 2. 8.

entries.title: Proverbs 17:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 13. 5.

y Because he is sensible of his own folly, and therefore forbears to speak le[illegible]t he should discover it; which is a great point of true Wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, He that separateth himself seeketh according to his desire, and intermeddleth in every business.

a According to this interpretation the sense is, Through desire (of it, to wit, of Wisdom, which is easily understood out of the end of the verse; such Ellipses being frequent in Scripture) a man having separated himself (being sequestred from the company, and noise, and business of the World, betaking himself to retirement and solitude, as men do that apply themselves to any serious study) seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom, i. e. useth all diligence, that he may search and find out all solid knowledg and true Wisdom. And this earnest desire and endeavour to get true Wisdom within a mans self is fitly opposed to the fools contempt of Wisdom, or to his desire of it, not for use and benefit but only for vain ostentation, which is expressed in the next verse. Although coherence is little regarded by Interpreters in the several Verses and Proverbs of this Book. But this verse is otherwise rendred in the margin of our English Bible, and by divers others, He that separateth himself (either 1. From his friend. Or rather 2. From other men, who affects singularity is wedded to his own Opinion, and through self-conceit despiseth the opinions and conversation of others) seeketh according to his desire (seeketh to gratifie his own Inclinations and Affections, and chuseth those opinions which most comply with them) and intermeddleth (for this word is used in a bad sense, Prov. [illegible]7. 14. & 20. 3. and it is not found elsewhere, save in this place) in every business, as proud and singular persons are commonly pragmatical, delighting to find faults in others, that they may get some Reputation to themselves by it. Heb. in every thing that is, thrusting themselves into the actions and affairs of other men Or, as this last clause is and may be rendred, and contendeth (Heb. mingleth himself; for words of that signification are commonly used for contending or fighting, as Deut. 2. 5, 9, 19. Isa. 36. 8 Dan. 11 10.) with or against (for the Hebrew prefix, beth, oft signifies against) all Reason or Wisdom: whatsoever any man speaketh against his opinion and desire, though it be never so reasonable and evident, he rejecteth it, and obstinately maintains his own opinion.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
b In getting [illegible]ound and saving knowledg, either by his own s[illegible]udy, or by the instructions of wise and good men.

c Heb. but (his delight is) in the discovery of his own heart, i. e. in uttering that folly and wickedness which is in his heart: being more forward to speak than to hear, which is one badge of a fool.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Into any place or company.

e Either 1. Passively; he is justly contemned and reproached by those who converse with him. Or rather 2. Actively; he despiseth and scorneth all Instruction and Reproof, neither fearing God, nor reverencing Man: For he seems here to note his sin, rather than his punishment.

f And he doth not only contemn others in his heart, but sheweth his contempt of them by ignominious and reproachful expressions and carriages.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 20. 5.

g i. e. A wise mans, as the next clause explains this, who is worthy of the name, and hath the understanding of a man in him. This Hebrew word oft-times notes an eminent or excellent person, and therefore is opposed to Adam, which designs any ordinary man.

h Full of deep Wisdom

i That Wisdom which is in his heart is continually pouring forth wise and good counsels.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Lev. 19. 15. Deut. 1. 17. & 16. 19. Chap. 24. 2[illegible].

k i. e. It is a most wicked and hateful thing. See on Prov. 17. 15, 26.

l To favour his unrighteous cause.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m A fool by his rash and wicked speeches provoketh others to quarrel with him, and, as it follows, to strike him.

n Procureth strokes to himself.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12. 18. & 26. 22.

Or, whisperer.

o Who privily slandereth his Neighbour.

Or, like as

p Deeply wound the Reputation, and afterwards the Heart, of the slandered person. Compare Prov. 12. 18. Or, as others render the word, are as smooth or flattering, i. e. they really are so; the particle as, being oft used to express the truth of the thing, as hath been noted before. See also Ioh. 1. 14. They are softer than Oil, as is said Psal. 55. 21. For slanderers use to cover and usher in their calumnies with pretences of kindness and compassion to them whom they traduce.

Or, but. when men are wounded.

Heb. Chambers.

q They wound mortally, piercing to the very heart, which is oft meant by the belly, as Iob 15. 35. & 32. 19. &c.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: r They are alike, though they take several paths, yet both come to one end, even to extream want and poverty.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] Sam. 22. [illegible] Psal. 18. 2. [illegible] 1. & 61. [illegible] 91. 2. & [illegible] [illegible]

s i. e. The Lord, as he hath revealed himself in his works, and especially in his word by his Promises, and the Declarations of his infinite perfections, and of his goodwill to his people.

t Is sufficient for our Protection in case of the greatest dangers.

u Which limitation he adds to beat down the vain confidences of those men, who though they live in a gross neglect and contempt of God will expect Salvation from him.

[illegible] is set [illegible]

entries.title: Proverbs 18:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 10. 15.

u He trusts to his Wealth, as that which will either enable him to resist his enemy, or at least purchase his favour.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 11. 2.

x Pride is a cause and presage of ruine, as is noted Prov. 16. 18.

y Or, goeth. This clause we had, Prov. 15. 33.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] returne[illegible] [illegible].

z Before he hath fully heard and considered what another is speaking about it.

a It is a shameful folly, though he seek the reputation of a wise man by it, as if he could readily and throughly understand all that another can say before he hath uttered it.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
b i. e. The soul, to wit, which is unwounded, as appears by the opposite branch of the verse, which is vigorous and chearful, supported by the sense of Gods Love, and the Conscience of its own Integrity, and the prospect of its present Peace, and future Happiness.

c Will easily support him under any bodily or outward troubles, as Gods people have oft found by experience.

d Dejected with the sense of its own guilt and misery.

e It is most grievous and intollerable without divine assistance.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f By employing his thoughts and studies upon it.

g By a greedy and diligent attention to those from whom he may learn it.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 17. 8. [illegible] [illegible]1. 14.

h Procures him free access to great men. Heb. enlargeth him, as this very Phrase is rendred, Psal. 4. 1. and elsewhere, freeth him from straits and oppressions.

i Gets him favour and free conversation with them.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k He that first pleadeth his cause.

l Both to himself and to the Judg or Court, by his fair pretences.

m To contend with him in judgment, and to plead his cause.

n Examineth the truth and weight of his Allegations, and disproveth them, and detecteth his weakness. Or, discovers him: for seeking or searching are oft put for finding, as Prov. 17. 9, 19. and elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o By determining the matters in difference.

p Maketh a partition, giveth to every one what is right or meet, by the disposition of divine Providence.

q So it doth also between mean persons, but he mentions the mighty because they are most prone to contention, and most fierce and intractable in it, and most capable of doing great mischief to themselves and others by it, and therefore they most need this remedy.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r To wit, by his Brothers unkindness or injury.

s Or, is stronger, which is sufficiently understood by the mention of a strong City, to which he is compared; such Ellipses being frequent in the Hebrew, as hath been noted before.

t Which is hardly to be conquered.

u Which are very strong, and not to be broken, and make the castle strong, and hardly to be won. The truth of this assertion is confirmed by the testimony of Aristotle and other learned Authors, who affirm the same thing; and the reason of it is evident, because the nearness of the Relation greatly heightens the provocation, and Love abused frequently turns to extream hatred.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12. 14. & 13. 2.

x Wise and edifying discourses tend to the comfort and satisfaction of the Speaker, as well as to the good of the Hearers.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y Are brought upon men by the good or bad use of their tongues.

z Either 1. The Tongue, that love and use much talking, which is oft censured as a sin, and a cause of mischief. See Prov. 10. 19. Iam. 1. 19. Or 2. The use of their tongue in either of those ways, which are plainly supposed in the former clause of the verse: they who do not only speak well, which a wicked man may somtimes do, or speak ill, which a good man may possibly do, but do love, and therefore accustom themselves to speak well or ill.

a Shall receive either good or evil according to the quality of their Speeches.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 19. 14.

b Either 1. Simply a Wife; for a Wife, though she be not the best of kind, is to be esteemed a blessing, being useful both for society of life, Gen. 2. 18. and for the mitigation of a mans cares and troubles, and for the prevention of sins. Or 2. Good Wife, one that deserves the Name, and performs the duty of that Relation, a wise and worthy Wife, as this word may seem to imply, being deduced from the Hebrew word, isch, which somtimes notes a man of Eminency. And this limitation and explication of the word may be gathered both from the following commendations, which would hardly be given to a bad Wife, and from the usage of Scripture in which this Ellipsis is frequent, as a path or way is put for a good path or way, Psal. 119. 1. Prov. 15. 10. an answer for a good answer, Prov. 15. 23. a King for a good King, Prov. 16. 10. & 29. 4. a name for a good name, Prov. 22. 1. Eccles. 7. 1. &c.

c A singular Blessing.

d Obtaineth her not by his own Wit, or Art, or Diligence, but by Gods good Providence towards him, which ordereth that and all other events as it pleaseth him.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e Humbly begs the favour of rich men, as his necessities and occasions require it.

Jam. 2. 3.

f Speaketh proudly and scornfully either to the poor, or to others that converse with him, being puffed up with a conceit of his Riches, and of his self-sufficiency.

entries.title: Proverbs 18:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Heb. A man of friends: either 1. Who desires the friendship of others. Or 2. Who professeth friendship to others.

Ch. 17. 17.

h To him that desires and needs his help: who is more hearty in the performance of all friendly Offices.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 28. 6.

a Who is upright in his words and actions.

b That useth to speak wickedly, which proceeds from a wicked heart, and is usually attended with an evil Life.

c Is an Hypocrite, or a wicked man, for this is opposed to the upright man in the former clause; yea, though he be rich, which is implied from the same clause.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Which is the principal cause and director of all mens actions.

e Without Wisdom or Prudence to discern his way, and what, and how, he ought to act in his several cases and concernments.

f It is very evil and pernicious.

g That rashly and headily rusheth into actions without serious consideration. So two vices are here censured, the want of Knowledg, and the neglect or di[illegible]use of Knowledg in a mans actions.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h Either 1. enticeth him to sin. Or rather 2. Crosseth and blas[illegible]eth his designs and enterprises, and brings losses and miseries upon him.

i He ascribes his unhappiness not to his own sin and folly, which is the true cause of it, but to God and his Providence, against which he unjustly murmurs.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 14. 20.

k Is disowned and forsaken by those who are most obliged to help him.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ver. 9. Exod. 23. 1. Deut. 19. 16, 19. Ch. 6. 19. & 21. 28.

Heb. held innocent.

l Though he escape the observation and punishment of men, yet he shall not avoid the judgment of God.

m That accustometh himself to lying, either in judgment, or in common conversation.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. face.

n Or, as others, of the liberal or bountiful man: which comes to the same thing: for Kings were antiently called Benefactors, Luk. 22. 25.

o Not sincerely, as daily experience shews, but in shew or profession, or in the outward expressions of it, whereby they may oblige him.

Heb. a man of gifts.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 14. 20.

p His nearest and dearest Relations, who are oft called Brethren in Scripture, by a common Synecdoche.

q i. e. Despise and shun him, as men do any thing which they hate, and as the following words explain it.

r His former companions, who in his prosperity professed friendship to him.
