s Earnestly imploring their pity. Or, he urgeth (Heb. pursueth) their words, i. e. alledgeth their former promises, and professions of Friendship. Or, without any supplement, he seeketh words, as the Preacher sought to find out acceptable words, Eccles. 12. 10. wherewith he might prevail or move them to pity.

t Heb. they are not, either 1. His Friends are not, to wit, what they pretended to be, friends to him. Or 2. Their words are vain, and without effect, there is no reality in them.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. an heart.

u Or, loveth himself, because he procures great good to his Soul, or to himself, as it follows, as sinners on the contrary are said to hate their Souls, Prov. 29. 24. because they bring mischief upon them.

x That observeth and carefully practiseth its precepts, as that Phrase is commonly used.

y Shall have great benefit by it, both for his conduct in this Life, and for his happiness in the next.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: z This was said before, v. 5. and seems to be here repeated, either for its great use and weight in humane society, and to shew how much God abhors such practices; or to shew the pernicious effects of this sin, and consequently of all other sins, one eminent kind being put for all the rest, and this in opposition to the good effects of Wisdom or Piety, which he declared in the foregoing verse.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Eccl. 10. 6.

a To live in Pleasure, and Plenty, and outward Glory.

Ch. 30. 22. Eccl. 10. 7.

c Who is of a servile condition and disposition, not much differing from a Fool, who is a servant to his Lusts, and wholly unfit to rule other men.

d i. e. Over men of better quality than himself: for servants are commonly ignorant, and when they are advanced they grow insolent, and presumptuous, and intolerable.

b It doth not become him, nor suit with him, partly because Prosperity corrupts even wise men, and makes fools mad, and partly because it gives him more opportunity to discover his folly, and to do mischief both to himself and others. He implies that a rod or punishment is fitter for him than pleasure, as is noted, Prov. 10. 13. & 26. 3.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 14. 29.

Or, prudence.

e This is opposed to the perverse judgment of worldly men who account it [illegible]olly and stupidity, not quickly to resent a provocation, and a dishonour and reproach not to revenge it.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 16. 1[illegible], 15. & 2[illegible]. 2. & 28. 15.

[illegible] [illegible].

[illegible]

entries.title: Proverbs 19:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 10. 1. & 15. 20. & 17. 21, 25.

Ch. 21. [illegible] [illegible] & 27. 15.

f Are like rain continually dropping upon an house which by degrees marreth the House and Houshold stuff, and driveth the inhabitants out of it. He compareth her to a continual dropping, because of that inseparable Union and necessary cohabitation of Husband and Wife together, notwithstanding such contentions.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 18. 22.

g Is vouchsafed to a man by a singular providence of God, who is the only Searcher and Ruler of hearts, exactly discerning who are prudent or pious, in which even wise mens judgments are commonly mistaken, and inclining the minds and hearts of persons one towards another.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h Maketh a man careless and negligent, and like one asleep in his business, whereby he cometh to want, as it follows.

Chap. 1[illegible] [illegible] & 20. 13.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Luk. 11. 28.

i The commands of God called by way of eminency the commandment, as the Word is oft used Emphatically for the word of God, as hath been noted before.

k Either 1. His own ways, by not taking heed to his ways, so as to order his Conversation aright. Or 2. The ways of God, who is understood in the former clause.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Mat. 10 42. & 25. 40. 2 Cor. 9. 6, 7.

l Who takes what is done to them as done to himself, because it is done to them whom God, as to this particular, hath put in his own stead, to be his receivers, and whom God hath in a peculiar manner commended to the care and charity of all other men.

Or, his deed.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 13. 24. & 23. 13.

m Before custom in sin, and thy indulgence hath made him hard-hearted and incorrigible.

n Forbear not to give him due and necessary correction.

Or, to his [illegible], or, to cause him to die.

o Which o[illegible]t stirs up a foolish and pernicious pity in Parents towards them. This word, with some small difference in the points, is used in this sense, Isa. 14. 11. Or, as it is in the margent, to his destruction, intimating that this is a cruel pity, and a likely way to expose him to that death threatned to stubborn Sons, Deut. 21. 18, 21. But this clause is, and may be, rendred otherwise, yet, or but do not lift up thy soul (which signifies a vehement desire, Deut. 24. 15. Psal. 25. 1. Ier. 44. 14. let not thy passion, or eager desire of chastening him, transport thee so far as) to cause him to die, i. e. use moderation in this work.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p Or, He who is of great wrath, of strong passions. Which may be understood either 1. More particularly, of a Son of such a temper, who is very impatient of correction, and breaks forth into violent passions upon that occasion; and then the following words contain the Parents duty, which is to take care to punish him, because if he spare him that time for his passion, he must do so again and again, the same cause returning upon him, and so must wholly forbear to chasten him. Or 2. More generally, of any man of a fierce and furious temper and carriage, and then the next words declare only the event, by his great and repeated provocations he will bring punishment upon himself either from God or Men.

q If either a Parent, or another person provoked by him, forbear to punish him. He turneth his speech to the party, as is usual in Scripture, and in other Authors.

Heb. add.

r Heb. thou must add, to wit, to deliver him again and again, as oft as he shall offend: or, thou wilt add or encrease, to wit, his wrath, which thou shouldst subdue.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 55. 23.

s Before thy Death come. Which he adds not exclusively, as if he ought not to be wise before, but Emphatically to shew, that how foolishly soever he had spent his former and younger years, it highly concerned him to be wise before it was too late, or before Death came.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job. 23. 13. Psal. 33. 10, 11. Chap. 16. 1, 9. Isa. 46. 10. Heb. 6. 17.

t Understand out of the opposite Clause, which shall not stand but be disappointed.

u His eternal (and unchangeable and most wise Decree, which oft-times contradicts, and always over-rules the designs and purposes of men.

x i. e. Be certainly fulfilled, as this Phrase is used, Ier. 44. 28, 29. and elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y Either 1. of any or every Man. All men desire, and it is desirable to be in a capacity of being kind and bountiful to others, whereby they gain love and honour, and many other great advantages. Or 2. of the poor man, expressed in the next Clause. The hearty will or desire of being kind or liberal to others in necessity is all the kindness which a poor Man can shew, and is accepted by God, and should be owned by men as a real kindness. Compare 2 Cor. [illegible]. 12. Or 3. of the rich Man, as may be gathered from the opposition of this Man to the poor Man in the following Clause; such Ellipses being very common in this Book, as hath been noted again and again. So the sense may be this, There be a sort of rich men all whose kindness and charity consists in good desires and well-wishes to Persons in misery, saying to them, depart in p[illegible]ace, be ye warmed and filled, but not giving them those things which are needful, as it is expressed, Iam. 2. 16. And this sense seems to agree very well with the following Clause. But being singular in this exposition, I submit it to the judicious Reader.

z Who is not able to give what he desires to do.

a Than a rich Man who feeds the poor with good words and fair promises, but doth not perform what he pretends, and is able to do.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: b shall want nothing, and shall be fully contented with God's favour and blessing. With any destructive affliction.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 1[illegible] 1[illegible]. [illegible] 13. 15.

d Either to keep it warm in cold Weather: Or, to give it rest, being loth to oppress it with the labour of any action. It is a sarcastical Hyperbole.

e To wit, to feed himself; he expects that the Meat should drop into his Mouth.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 21. 11.

f An obstinate and impudent Transgressor, who rejects and scorns all admonitions, and therefore is to be taught with blows.

g Who sin through ignorance, and imprudence, and infirmity, being possibly drawn to sin by the scorners evil counsel or example.

[illegible] will be [illegible].

h A verbal reproof will be more effectual for his reformation than the severest punishments will be to a scorner.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i i. e. His Fathers estate by unjust or riotous courses.

k Causeth her to avoid and abhor his presence and society, and to go from the House where he is.

l Both to himself and to his Parents and Family. But this Verse may very well be rendred otherwise, the last words being made the subject of the Proposition, as is usual in Scripture, A Son that causeth shame and bringeth reproach (upon himself and his friends by wicked ways) wasteth his Fathers (estate and health and comfort) and chaseth or driveth away his Mother. These are the effects of his wickedness.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: m If thou hast formerly, yet do not now any longer hearken to those false Doctrines or evil counsels which tend to withdraw thee from the belief or practice of God's holy Word.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. a wit [illegible] of Beli[illegible]l.

n Hath no reverence to the place of Justice, nor to the presence of God there, nor to that Sacred and Solemn Work of executing Judgment, but in spight of all gives in a false Testimony

o Uttereth wickedness with as great greediness, and delight, and ease, as they swallow down delicious Meats and Drinks. Compare Iob 15. 16.

entries.title: Proverbs 19:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: p Either by men, or at least by God; although they be deferred for a time, yet they are treasured up for them, and shall infallibly be inflicted upon them.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Wine immoderately drunk makes men mockers or scoffers at God and men. Compare Hos. 7. 5.

b Makes men full of rage and passion.

c Is a Fool, or a mad Man, because he depriveth himself of the use of his reason.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 16. 14. & 19. 12.

d Passively taken, the terror which the wrath of a King causeth, by comparing this with Ch. 19. 12.

e Exposeth himself to manifest danger of Death.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 17. 14.

f Either to prevent it, or, if it be begun, to put an end to it: which, although proud and profane Persons esteem dishonourable to them, is indeed their glory, because it is an evidence of their great wisdom and power over their passions, and of their respect and obedience to their Soveraign Lord, in which their Honour and Happiness consists.

g To wit, with matters of strife, he is always ready to begin strife, and obstinate in the continuance of it.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 10. 4.

Or, Winter.

h Of the Plowing season, which is in Autumn and towards Winter. He hates and avoids all laborious and difficult work, although his own necessity and interest oblige him to it.

i And not obtain an Alms not in that time of Plenty and bounty, because mens Hearts are justly hardned against that Man who by his own sloth and wilfulness hath brought himself to want.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 18. 4.

k Either 1. Wisdom or ability to give good Counsel. Or 2. Designs or purposes of doing somthing of moment: for this word is frequently used in both senses but the last seems fittest here.

l Either 1. is there in great abundance. Or 2. is secret and hard to be discovered.

m By prudent Questions and Discourses, and a diligent Observation of his words and actions.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, bounty.

n Most men are forward to profess Religion, and speak of their own good deeds.

o One who is indeed what he seemeth and professeth himself to be.

p There are but few such to be found.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q He proveth himself to be so not onely by his profession, of which he spoke in the former Verse, but by his sincere and unblameable conversation.

Ps. 112. 2.

r By vertue of that Covenant which God hath made with such men, which is not confined to their Persons, but entaileth Blessings upon their Posterity.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 16. 10. Vers. 26.

s That makes it his great care and business to execute Judgment and Justice among his People, especially if he do this in his own Person, as was usual in ancient Times, and sees things with his own Eyes. As for the Phrase, the sign or gesture is here put for the thing signified by it.

t Effectually punisheth and suppresseth all wickedness.

u With his very looks, or by his diligent inspection into affairs.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
1 Kin. 8. 46. 2 Chr. 6. 36. Job 14. 4. Ps. 51. 5. Eccles. 7. 20. 1 Ioh. 1. 8.

x No Man living upon Earth can say this truly and sincerely. Compare 1 Kings 8. [illegible]6. Iob 14. 4. & 15. 14. Eccles. 7. 21. 1 Ioh. 1. 8.

y I am perfectly free from all guilt and filth of sin in my Heart and Life.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Vers. 23. Deut. 25. 13, &c. Ch. 11. 1. & 16. 11. Mic. 16. 1[illegible]

Heb. a stone and a stone.

Heb. an Ephah, and an Ephah.

z One greater and truer for publick shew, and one lesser and false for private use, when they had an opportunity of deceiving.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Young Children discover their inclinations or dispositions even by their childish speeches and carriages, as not having yet learnt the art of dissembling.

b Or rather, will be; for it is not expressed in the Hebrew, and therefore may be either way supplied. The sense is, The future disposition and conversation of a Man may very probably be conjectured from his childish manners.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 4. 11. Ps. 94. 9.

c It is God alone who gives us our Senses and Natural faculties, and the use and exercise of them, and especially a power of employing them aright to see and observe the works of God, and to hear and receive his Word and all wholesom instructions. Whence he leaves it to us to gather, that God doth exactly see and hear all mens words, and actions though never so secret. He names the Eye, and Ear, because these are the two Senses by which instructions are conveyed to the mind; but under them he seems to comprehend all other senses and powers of Soul or Body, by a Synecdoche.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 6. 9. & 12. 14. & 19. 15.

d i. e Immoderate sleep, or sloth or idleness. Take sleep because necessity requires it, not from any love to it.

e Awake out of sleep, shake off sloth and betake thy self to thy employment with diligence and vigor.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f The commodity is but of little worth.

g To wit, to the Seller: he discommends it that he may bring down the price of it.

h With the commodity purchased.

i That by his wit he hath over-reached the Seller, and got a great advantage to himself. This he notes as a common but reprovable practice.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k To wit, in the World, in divers mens hands, by whom it is highly prized.

Ch. 3. 15. & 8. 11.

l But wise speeches proceeding from an understanding or honest Heart are of far greater worth and use, both to him that uttereth them and to those that receive and improve them to their own benefit.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 22. 27. & 27. 13.

m To wit, as a Pledge, without which he ought not to be trusted, because by this action he sheweth himself to be a Fool, and he taketh the ready way to beggery. Obj. This precept contradicts that Law which forbad the taking of a Garment for a Pledge, Exod. 22. 26. Answ.. It doth not contradict it, for the cases vastly differ; for that Law concerned onely the Poor, who were forced to borrow for their own necessity, and therefore deserve pity; whereas this reacheth onely those who are or would be thought rich and sufficient Security for others, and who borrow not for their own need, but for a meer Stranger, for which folly they deserve to be severely punished. Besides, this may be onely a Prediction, though it be delivered in the form of a Precept, as many Predictions are; and so shews what may be expected by him that is guilty of such folly, even that he shall be stripped of his Garments and other necessaries.

n For a Forreigner or a Person unknown to him.

o That is surety: which words are to be understood out of the foregoing Clause.

p For an Harlot, who is so called, Prov. 2. 16. and elsewhere.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 9. 17.

Heb. bread of lying, or, falshood.

q Gain or pleasure procured by unrighteous courses.

r It shall be bitter and pernicious at last like grit[illegible]y Bread, which offends the Teeth and Stomach: it will certainly bring upon him the horrours of a guilty Conscience, and the wrath and judgments of the Almighty God.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 15. 22.

s The way to bring our purposes and desires to a good effect, is to manage them with serious consideration and good advice.

t Or, therefore. This is necessary in every common undertaking, and much more in a thing of such high importance as War is.

Ch. 24. 6.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 11. 13.

u He that delighteth in and accustometh himself to the practice of spreading Tales or evil Reports, will not forbear to publish the greatest secrets which are committed to his trust. Or, as others render it, and as the words lie in the Hebrew Text, He that revealeth secrets (contrary to his promise or the trust reposed in him, you may by that token be assured that) he doth and will go about as a Tale-bearer. He who divulgeth secrets cannot or will not forbear to publish other things, and so is not fit to be trusted with any thing.

x To prevent that mischief. Heb. and. So the following Sentence is not inferred from the former, but onely added to it.

y Avoid frequent and familiar society and conversation with him.

Or, inticeth.

z By which artifice he seeks to gain thy affections, and so to fish out all thy secrets, which he may impart to others whom he may oblige hereby, and so render his company more acceptable.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 21. 17. Lev. 20. 9. Mat. 15. 4.

a Heb. and; which is used for or, Exod. 12. 5. Levit. 6 3. and elsewhere.

Or, Candle.

b His comfort and happiness, his Name and Memory which are oft compared in Scripture to a Lamp or Light.

c Shall utterly perish; he shall die Childless, and with Ignominy.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 28. 20.

d An Estate somtimes is got suddenly in the very beginning of a Man's labours for it, in which case it may be presumed that some undirect and unrighteous courses were used, for the getting of it, because Riches are very seldom given by God, or gotten by men, without mens diligence. But this, as well as many other Proverbs, are to be understood of the common course, although it admit of some exceptions. For somtimes Merchants or others get great Estates speedily by one happy Voyage, or by some other prosperous event. This Translation follows the Hebrew Marginal reading, but according to the Textual reading, it may be thus rendered and understood, An Inheritance gotten in the beginning (to wit, of a mans indeavours) is abominable, to wit, unto God, being supposed to be unjustly gotten, as was now said.

e At last it shall be cursed and wither by God's just judgment.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 32. 35. Ch. 17. 13. & 24. 29. Rom. 12. 17 1 Thess. 5. 15. 1 Pet. 3. 9.

f In thy Heart: give not way to any such evil Thoughts or Purposes.

g To whom it belongs to execute vengeance, and to deliver his People from all their Enemies.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Vers. 10.

h Of which see above on v. 10.

Heb. balances of deceit.

i Is very wicked and hateful to God and men.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 37. 23. Ch. 16. 9. Jer. 10. 23.

k All mens purposes and actions.

l Are ordered and over-ruled by God's wise and powerful Providence to accomplish his own counsel and good pleasure, and not what men list or intend

m Either 1. what course he ought to take; which he cannot know without God's direction and assistance, Compare Prov. 16. 9. Ier. 10. 23. Or 2. what the issue of his designs will be, whether they shall succeed or be disappointed, the way being taken for the end or event to which it leads, as it is in many other places. The scope of the Proverb is to shew, that all the events of humane life are neither ordered nor foreseen by Mans, but onely by God's Providence, and therefore men should onely mind the doing of their duty, and then quietly depend upon God for a good Issue to their endeavours.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n It brings guilt and God's curse and vengeance upon him.

o i. e. Those Meats or Drinks which were devoted or consecrated to God. Under which one kind he comprehends and forbids all alienation of Sacred or Dedicated things from God to a Man's private use or benefit: Of which see Levit. 27. 9. Deut. 23. 21. Mal. 3 8, 9. Act. 5. 1, &c.

p After a Man hath made Vows to consider whether he can possibly, or may lawfully keep them, and to invent or enquire of others all ways possible to break his Vow, and to satisfie or deceive his Conscience in so doing. Which enquiry is justly censured as a sin and snare, because it is an evidence of a covetous or irreligious Mind, and is the ready way and first step towards the open violation of it.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 101. 5, &c. Vers. 3.

q Who seriously minds his Duty and his true interest.

r Breaks their Companies and Consederacies, and forceth them to flee several ways for their own safety, driveth them from his presence, and from the Society of honest men, as the Chaff is by the Husbandman separated from the Corn, and driven away by the Wind, of which this Hebrew word is commonly used; and to which the next Clause hath some reference.

s As the Cart-wheel was anciently turned over the Sheaves to beat the Corn out of them, Isa. 28. 27, 28. He punisheth them severely, as their Offences deserve. This or such like punishments were not unusual among the Eastern Nations, as we may gather from, 2 Sam. 8. 2. & 12. 31 Amos 1. 3.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t i. e. The reasonable Soul.

Or, lamp.

u Is a clear and glorious light set up in Man for his information and direction.

x So called partly because it comes from God in a more immediate and peculiar manner than the Body doth, Eccles. 12. 7. and partly because it is in Gods stead to observe and judge all a Man's actions.

y Discerning not onely his outward actions, which are visible to others, but his most inward and secret thoughts and affections, which no other Man can see, 1 Cor. 2. 11. The Belly is here put for the Heart, as it is frequently. The Soul can reflect upon and judge of its own dispositions and actions. Which plainly sheweth that the Heart is not so deceitful, but that a Man by diligent study of it, and the use of the means appointed by God, may arrive at a certain knowledge of its state and condition, in reference to God, and to Salvation.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 101. 1. Ch. 29. 14.

z Clemency to Offenders, and bounty to worthy, and to indigent Persons.

a Faithfulness in keeping his Word and Promises inviolably.

b Because they engage God to guard him, and gain him the reverence and affections of his People, which is a Kings greatest safety and happiness.

c Which is again mentioned, to shew that although it be an act of Grace, and therefore in some sort free, yet Princes are obliged to it both by their duty, and by their Interest, because it is a singular means of their preservation.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d That wherein they glory as their Priviledge above old men.

Ch. 16. 31.

e i. e. Their old Age expressed by the outward sign of it, wherein they glory as their peculiar Priviledge, as a Testimony of their Piety and God's Blessing, and as a token of their great experience and wisdom. The design of this Proverb is to declare the several advantages of several Ages and the mutual need they have one of another, and thereby to engage them to mutual love and assistance, and to friendly converse, and to make every one contented with his own Age and Condition, and not to envy nor yet despise his Brother or the difference of their Ages, as is very usual among men.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Grievous wounds which make men black and blew, or severe punishments.

Heb. is a [illegible] Medi [illegible] against [illegible]

g Are the most effectual means to reclaim a wicked Man, and to purge out his corruption.

h Heb. and stripes, which answer to the wounds in the former Clause.

i Either 1. Which pierce even to the inward parts of the Belly, and so we are to understand out of the former Branch, cleanse away evil. Or 2. They cleanse the inward parts of the Belly, i. e. of the Heart. So this is an addition to the former Clause, and the sense of the whole is, Grievous wounds or stripes do cleanse not only the outward Man by keeping it from evil actions, but even the inward Man, by expelling or subduing vile affections. Which is mentioned as a great and blessed benefit of afflictions.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a His very inward purposes and inclinations, which seem to be most in a Man's own power, and out of the reach of all others, and much more his Tongue and Hand, and all his outward actions. He names Kings hot to exclude other men, but because they are more arbitrary and uncontrollable than other men.

b Which Husbandmen or Gardiners can draw by little Channels into the adjacent grounds as they please, and as their occasions require.

c Directeth and boweth partly by suggesting those things to their Minds which have a commanding influence upon their wills, and partly by a direct and immediate motion of their wills and affections, which being God's Creatures must needs be as subject to his power and pleasure as either mens Minds or Bodies are, and which he moves sweetly and suitably to their own Nature, though strongly and effectually.

d So as they shall fulfil his counsels and designs, either of Mercy or of Correction to themselves, or to their People.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: e This was said, Ch. 16. 2. where it is explained, and is here repeated, either for the great importance and usefulness of it, or because he perceived that the Israelites were very prone to selfdeceit.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
1 Sam. 15. 22. Ch. 15. 8. Isa. 1. 11, &c. Hos. 6. 6. Mic. 6. 7, 8.

f The conscientious performance of all our duties to men.

g Than the most costly, outward services offered to God, joyned with the neglect of our Moral duties to God or men. The same thing is affirmed, 1 Sam. 15. 22. Hos. 6. 6. Mic. 6. 7, 8, &c.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 6. 17.

Heb. haughtiness of eyes.

h One gesture or sign of Pride put for all the rest. Prov. 6. 17.

i Pride lurking and reigning in the Heart, though it do not discover it self to men by outward actions, but be disguised with a shew of humility, as it is frequently.

Or, the light of the wicked.

k Either 1. strictly and properly so called: even their civil or natural actions, which in themselves are lawful and good, are made sinful as they are managed by ungodly men, without any regard to the service and glory of God, which ought to be the great end of all our actions, 1 Cor. 10. 31. and with a design of serving their own wicked lusts by it. Or 2. Metaphorically, their designs and endeavours, which are said to be sin, because they are wholly and fully set upon sin, and they make sin their trade or business, which is called Plowing wickedness, Job 4. 8. But all the ancient Interpreters, and divers others render the word the Lamp or Light, as this Hebrew word, even thus pointed, is rendred, 1 Kings 11. 36. & 15. 4. 2 Kings 8. 19. 2 Chron. 21. 7. and the Lamp of the wicked is a Phrase used in this Book, Ch. 13. 9. & 24. 20. as also, Iob 21. 17. whereas the Plowing of the wicked is a Phrase not elsewhere used. And this seems best to agree with the Context, for by their Lamp he seems to understand all their pomp and glory, that worldly greatness and Prosperity, which is the Fewel of their Pride, and therefore is most fitly joyned with it.

l It is by them turned into sin, and made the occasion of much wickedness. The whole Verse may be thus rendred, An high look, and a proud Heart, which is the light or glory of the wicked (i. e. wherein they glory, esteeming it magnanimity or gallantry of spirit) is sin, i. e. is a great and grievous sin. And in this manner the learned Mercer renders the Verse, save onely that he translates the Hebrew word Nir, the Plowing.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 10. 4

m Who carefully and industriously prosecutes what he hath wisely contrived and resolved,

n Who manageth his affairs rashly, without due consideration.

o Is likely to bring himself to po verty.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 10. 2. & 13. 11.

p By false-witness-bearing, or by any other false or deceitful words or actions, whereby many men get riches.

q Is like the Chaff or Smoak driven away by the Wind, it is neither satisfactory nor durable, but quickly vanisheth away, as hath been frequently observed of Estates ill-gotten.

r Not designedly but eventually, that take those courses which will bring Death or Destruction upon them or theirs.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. saw them, or, dwell with them.

s The injury which they do to others shall either by God or men be returned upon their own heads.

t They wilfully and obstinatly give up themselves to unrighteous practices.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u The course of his life.

x Of every Man, of Man by Nature and in his corrupt estate, of a wicked or, impure man, to whom the pure is opposed in the next Clause.

y Estranged from God and from Man's primitive Integrity, and from the rule of his actions, Reason and Scripture: in which respects wicked men are called strangers, Psal. 54. 3. Ezek. 44. 7. and elsewhere.

z But he whose Heart is pure and upright, his conversation is agreeable to it.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Vers. 19. Ch. 19. 13. & 25. 24. & 27. 15.

a To wit, alone in quietness, as appears from the opposite clause.

b Of the roof of the House, which in those Countries was flat and plain and habitable, but was exposed to all the injuries of the Weather.

Heb. a woman of contentions.

Heb. an house of Society.

c Or, in a common House, or, an House of Society, where Husband and Wise live together, or which is capable of many Friends or Companies.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Jam. 4. 5.

d His Heart is fully and earnestly set in him, as it is expressed, Eccles. 8. 11. to do evil, to work wickedness, to do mischief to others, to satisfie his own lusts, though it be with injury of others.

Heb. is not favoured.

e If he either dissuade him from his wickedness, or stand in the way of his Lusts. He spares neither friend nor foe.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f The honest or plainhearted man, as Chap. 19. 25. where this whole verse for the substance of it is contained and explained.

g Or, prospers, as this word is used, Prov. 17. 8. and elsewhere. So the sense of the verse is, The simple learn Wisdom, both from the punishment of wicked men, and from the prosperityof good men.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h He looketh through its present Power and Glory (which dazleth the Eyes of others) unto that ruine to which it is designed.

i Or, now, or that, this being the thing which he wisely considereth.

k Or, will overthrow in his due time, though for a season he bear with them.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Mat. 18. 30, &c.

l When they cry out by reason of Oppression or want, and beg relief from him.

m Unto God or Men, in his straits which God will bring upon him.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 17. 8. & 18. 16.

n To a person loffended and angry with us, as the following words shew.

o Which makes it more acceptable; for gifts openly given savour of ostentation in the giver, and cause some shame or contempt to the receiver.

p Secretly conveyed into his bosom. See on Prov. 17. 8. & 18. 16.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q The sense is either 1. He is highly pleased and delighted with it. Or 2. He reapeth much comfort and benefit by it, which is opposed to the following destruction: joy is put for matter or cause of joy

r To do what is just or good, for this is opposed to working of iniquity.

s Or, as others render it, terror or horror, opposite to joy.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t That forsaketh the rule of Gods word, and walketh after his own Lusts.

Heb. rest.

u Shall, without Repentance, be condemned to eternal Death or Damnation.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, sport.

x That gives up himself to the pursuit and enjoyment of sensual and immoderate pleasures.

y Takes the ready course to Poverty.

z Which are put for all delicious fare and luxurious feasting; for Wine and Oil were much used in Feasts in those parts.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 11. 8.

a The wicked shall be brought into those troubles which were either threatned by God, or designed by wicked men against the righteous, and by that means, as by a ransom, the righteous shall be delivered. Thus Achan was a ransom for Israel, Ios. 7. 26. and Haman for Mordecai.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ver. 9.

Heb. in the land of the desert.

b Understand, in a wide house, as it is expressed above, v. 9. and as the opposition here requires.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 112. 3.

c Wise-men lay up all necessary and desirable treasures for their own use, and for their Children, and Families. Oil is particularly mentioned, partly because that was a considerable part of their Wealth and Treasures in those Countries, of which see Deut. 7. 13. & 28. 40, 51. Iudg. 9. 9. Mic. 6. 15. &c. and partly to shew that his Providence reached not only to necessaries, but even to matters of just and lawful delight.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d That fervently desires, and diligently and constantly endeavours to attain to them, for such shall and will certainly obtain them.

e Living in the constant exercise of these virtues.

f Shall obtain from God, what is right and due to him, either from God by vertue of his gracious promise, or from men, whose hearts God will dispose to deal justly and kindly with him.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Eccl. [illegible]. 14. &c.

g Wisdom and policy is oft times more considerable and powerful than strength.

h The strongest forts to which the Citizens trust most for their defence.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 12. 13. & 18. 21.

i From offensive and provoking speeches.

k His person.

l Which a licentious and abusive Tongue frequently brings upon a man.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Instead of that respect and glory which he seeks by such courses, he shall be branded with the Title and Imputation of an arrogant and scornful person, which is most contemptible and hateful to Mankind.

Heb. in the wrath of pride.

n Who in the conduct of his affairs and dealings in the world, is not governed by Reason and Justice, but by his own Pride and Passions.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 13. 4.

o Either 1. Tormenteth him almost to death, whilst he passionately desires that which he sees he shall not enjoy, and will not take pains to procure. Or 2. Exposeth him to extream want, and so to death, or so such wicked courses for the supply of his wants, as bring him to an untimely death.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p The slothful man mentioned in the last verse. But because the Verses in this Book are for the most part independent one upon another, this clause is and may be otherwise rendred, There is that coveteth, &c. Or, the wicked (which may be understood from the opposition of the righteous in the next clause) coveteth, &c.

q Spends his whole time in vain and lazy desires, but will not labour to get any thing, either to [illegible] [illegible], or to give to others.

Psal. 1129.

r By Gods Blessing upon his [illegible] he procures enough, not onely for his own support, but also for the liberal relief of others.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 50. 9. Ch. 15. 8. Isa. 66. 3. Jer. 6. 20. Amos 5. 22.

s All the most glorious and costly services which they offer to God.

t God rejects and abhors them, because they are offered by such men, and in such manner as God justly abhors.

u Or, because, as all the antient Translators render it, the Hebrew particle, aph, being expletive: Or, even because; so the following clause gives the reason of the former Proposition.

Heb. in wickedness.

x With an hypocritical and impenitent Heart, or with a bad design, not in obedience to Gods Command, and with respect to his honour and service, but either to cover, or countenance, or promote some wicked intention or course, which, notwithstanding all his professions of Religion, he is resolved to prosecute.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 19. 5, [illegible].

Heb. [illegible] of lies.

y Heb. A witness of lies one who is forward to swear or speak false things, or such things as he hath not heard nor learned from others, nor seen, but devised in his own heart.

z Shall be severely punished either by God or Men, and shall be confounded and silenced, because none will for the future regard or credit his testimony.

a He who hears before he speaks, and witnesseth nothing but what he hath heard or seen, and knows to be true.

b Doth not contradict himself, but always affirmeth the same thing. Or, as most other Interpreters render the words, speaketh (or, may speak, dare speak freely and boldly) for ever, when lyars are cut off, he lives, and is in a capacity of speaking and bearing witness again and again, as occasion requires, as long as he lives, and his Testimony will be received.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Continueth in evil courses with obstinacy and impudence, in spight of all the Commands of God, or Counsels of Men.

Or, considereth.

d He ordereth his steps aright, and if at any time he goeth away, he doth not add Rebellion to his sin, nor persist in his errour, but considereth his ways, and turneth his feet to Gods testimonies, as David did, Psal. 119. 59. Or, considereth his way, remembring with grief and shame what he hath done, and taking better heed to himself for the future.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 9. 23.

e Which can prevail against the Counsel and Will of God.

entries.title: Proverbs 21:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 20. 7. [illegible] 17.

f Under which particular all warlike provisions are comprehended.

[illegible] 3. 8.

[illegible] [illegible]ictory.

g The success of the battle depends not upon any humane strength or art, but meerly upon Gods Providence, who gives the victory when and to whom he pleaseth, and oft times to those that have least reason to expect it. Compare Eccl. 9. 11.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 7. 1.

a Heb. name put for good name, as Eccl. 7. 2. the word good being easily understood out of the next clause, in which it is expressed in the Hebrew text. A good reputation amongst wise and good men.

b Partly because it is a most special blessing from God being appropriated to worthy persons, whereas God commonly throws away Riches upon the basest of men: partly because it gives a man that tranquillity and satisfaction of mind, and that content and comfort in his condition, which no Riches can purchase: and partly because as it is commonly an evidence of a mans Virtue and Piety, so it is accompanied with Gods Love and Favour, whereas Riches are oft given by God in wrath, and to the hurt of the owner.

[illegible] [illegible] is [illegible] [illegible], &c.

c Or, good Grace or Favour, a good Report among men, especially among good men, and that hearty Love and Kindness which attends upon it.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 29. 13.

d Either 1. In a way of hostility or opposition, as this word is somtimes used, the rich contemning and oppressing the poor, and the poor envying and purloining from the rich; and so the following words are a reason why that hostility should cease. Or 2. In the way of mutual converse, they live together, and need one another.

e Not only as they are men, but also as they are poor or rich, which difference comes wholly from Gods Providence. They have one common Creator, and Lord, and Judg, and the one cannot despise nor grudge at the other without a reflection upon God.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 14. 16. [illegible] [illegible]. 12.

f The Calamity or Judgment of God threatned, and approaching.

g Retireth to his strong Tower, mentioned Prov. 18. 10. by Prayer and Repentance, putteth himself under the Protection of the Almighty. Compare Isa. 26. 20.

h In their former road and course of sin, carelesly and securely, as Travellers do in a road where they apprehend no danger.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 112. 3.

Or, the re [illegible] of humi [illegible], &c.

i Or, because of humility: or, as many others render it, the reward of humility, that reward which God hath graciously promised, and will give to Humility; which is a grace of great price in Gods Eyes. See Isa. 57. 15. Iam. 4. 6.

k By which he distinguisheth true and Christian Humility from counterfeit and moral humility, because that ariseth from a deep sense of Gods greatness, and purity, and perfection, compared with our own meanness, and filthiness, and manifold imperfections, whereas this is quit[illegible] of another nature, and from other grounds.

l The comforts of this life, and the happiness of the next, both which are promised to Godliness, 1 Tim. 4. 8.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m The wicked by their evil courses expose themselves to many dangers and occasions both of sin and mischief.

n That taketh heed to himself, and to his actions, and to the saving of his Life and Soul.

o Either 1. Will avoid the society of such froward persons. Or 2. Shall by that circumspection preserve himself from those thorns, &c. with which the Pronoun, them, agrees in number.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible], ca[illegible]chise.

p Or, initiate or instruct.

[illegible]. i[illegible] his [illegible].

q Heb. [illegible] [illegible] to his way, i. e. either 1. according to his capacity. [illegible] 2. In that course or manner of life which thou would [illegible] him chuse and follow. Or, as one learned man renders it, in the beginning of his way, i. e. in his tender years, as soon as he is capable of instruction. Heb. in the mouth, &c. The mouth is oft put for the beginning or entrance of any place, as Gen. 29. 2. Ios. 10. 18. Prov. 8. 3. Dan. 6. 17.

r To wit, not easily and ordinarily. The impressions made in childish years will remain, as hath been observed by all sorts of learned Writers. But this, as other Proverbs of like nature, are not to be understood as if this were universally and necessarily true, which Experience confutes, but because it is so for the most part, except some extraordinary cause hinder it.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Jam. 2. 6.

s To wit, with rigor and Tyranny, taking advantage of his necessities.

Heb. to the man that lendeth.

t Is at his mercy, and therefore forced to comply with his pleasure. The design of the Proverb is partly to correct this miscarriage of the rich, and partly to oblige all men to diligence, whereby they may deliver themselves from this servitude.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job. 4. 8. Hos. 10. 13.

u Or, unrighteousness, whose common practice it is to wrong or oppress others.

x Or trouble or misery, as this word is commonly used, and as divers here render it. The mischief which he hath done to others shall be returned to him by Gods righteous sentence.

Or, and with the red of his [illegible] anger he shall be consumed.

y That power which he used with fury and cruelty shall be taken away from him.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
2 Cor. 9. 6.

Heb. good of eye.

z Heb. A good eye. He who looks upon the wants and miseries of others with compassion and kindness, as this Phrase is used, Mat. 20. 15. as an evil eye is put for one that beholds others with envy and unmercifulness, Deut. 15. 9. Prov. 23. 6. & 28. 22.

a Both by God and Men.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psa. 101. 5.

b Out of your society, avoid conversation with him.

c Who neither fears God, nor reverenceth Man, but scorns all admonitions, and minds only the pleasing of himself, and the gratifying of his own Lusts, which is the chief cause of most contentions.

d Wherewith he loads those that either oppose or admonish him.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psa. 101. 6. Chap. 16. 13.

e Who is plain hearted or sincere, and abhors dissimulation.

Or, and hath grace in his lips.

f From those gracious speeches which naturally and commonly flow from a pure heart. Or, and (understand, loveth, out of the former clause) grace of his lips. Whose discourse is gracious and sincere.

g The greatest men will, or should, desire, and highly prize the acquaintance and advice of such persons, rather than of Dissemblers and Flatterers, wherewith they are most commonly pestered.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h God by the watchful Eye of his Providence maintains and defends.

i To wit, men of knowledge, the abstract being put for the concrete, as Pride is put for a proud man, Psal. 36. 11. Deceit for the deceitful, as Prov. 12 17. So here Knowledge for knowing and good men, such as the last verse spoke of, whose hearts are pure, and speeches gracious, not only the King shall be their friend, as he said there, but God also, which he adds here.

Or, the matters.

k Their false and flattering speeches, whereby they designed and expected to gain the favour and friendship of great men, which are opposed to the sincere and gracious speeches of good men, implied in the first clause of this verse, and expressed in the foregoing verse, Or, as others render it, and the word is very commonly used, the matters, all his Counsels, Hopes, Enterprizes, and Concerns.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 26. 13.

l Alledgeth as his excuse to them who upbraid him with idleness, or persuade him to diligence.

m There are extream dangers and invincible difficulties in my way.

n By that Lion, or some other way.

o Which is added to shew the ridiculousness of his excuse; for Lions abide in the woods or fields, nor in the streets of Towns or Cities.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 2. 16. & 5. 3. & 7. 5[illegible] & 23. 27.

p Her fair and flattering speeches wherewith she enticeth him to gross filthiness, as it is noted, Prov. 7. 21.

q Into which it is easie to fall, but hard, if not impossible, to get out of it. It is a rare thing for any person, once entred into the course of Whoredom, sincerely to repent of it, and turn from it. See Prov. 2. 19.

r To wit, in an high and singular manner, who by his former impieties, and contempt of God and of his Grace, hath provoked God to leave and loth him, and to punish one sin with another: for otherwise all sinners, as such, are abhorred by God.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
s Is fixed and setled there, as being born with him, and rooted in his very nature, and not plucked up without great difficulty and diligence.

Ch. 13. 24. & 19. 18. & 23. 13. & 29. 15, 17.

t The smart of punishment makes him weary of his sin, and watchful against it.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: u That vainly and prodigally casts away his estate upon those who do not need it, or gives it to them with evil design, as that they may assist him in oppressing the poor, or at least not hinder him in it.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
x Of wise and holy men of God.

y Thirst after it, and give up thy self to the diligent study of it.

z The knowledge of God, and of thy several duties, which I am here delivering to thee.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a The words of the wise.

Heb. in thy belly. Job 15. 35. & 32. 18.

b Heb. in thy belly, i. e. in thine heart, which implies receiving them in Love, and retaining them in mind and memory.

c Be fitly expressed: or, be disposed or ordered. The sense is, when thou hast got them into thine heart thou wilt be able and ready to discourse pertinently and profitably of them.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d That knowing God, and his word, and Promises, thou maist chearfully and confidently trust in him, which is the only way to thy safety and happiness.

Them.

Or, trust thou also.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. things of command or authority.

e Or, princely things, as they are called, Prov. 8. 6. the great things of Gods law, as Hos. 8 12.

f Consisting of Counsels to direct thy practice, and Knowledg to inform and enrich thy mind. Or, by that known Figure Hendiadis, in counsels of knowledg, i. e. in good counsels which proceed from sound knowledge, and make a man knowing and wise, which are opposed to the counsels of the wicked, Prov. 12. 5. which are without knowledg.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g That I may teach thee, not false, or vain, or uncertain things, as the Teachers of the Heathen Nations do, but the true and infallible Oracles of God.

h That being instructed by me, thou maist be able to give true, and solid, and satisfactory answers.

Or, to those that send thee.

i To wit, for thine advice in great and difficult matters. Or, to those that send thee, i. e. that employ thee in any business of moment, whereof they expect an account from thee.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k This may be mentioned, either 1. As a motive to this Robbery, because he was unable to resist him, or to revenge himself upon him: Do not take advantage of his Poverty. Or 2. As an Argument against it, because he is a fitter object for thy pity and Charity, than for thy Injustice or Cruelty. It is base and inhumane to crush such a person.

Zech. 7. 10.

l In the place of Judgment, or under pretence of Justice, and much less in other ways where there is no colour of Justice.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 23. 1[illegible].

m Which he hath in a peculiar manner undertaken to do.

n Take away not only their goods but their Lives too So fully will he recompence their wickedness to them.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: o Into his company: not converse frequently and familiarly with him, as friends use to do.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p Lest thou be instructed or provoked by his passion to return the like to him.

q Either 1. A mischief, which is oft the effect of unbridled rage. Or 2. An occasion of sin, either by drawing thee to an imitation or requital of his rage; or by tempting thee to unfaithfulness in performing the great office of a Friend, to wit, Admonition or reproof, which, by reason of his furious temper, thou either canst not, or wiltst not do.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 6. & 11. 15.

r To wit, rashly, or unnecessarily.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 20. 1

s Why wiltst thou put thy self into the hands of such a man, who will exact the debt from thee without any compassion? For though God did not allow this practice, covetous Creditors would frequently do it.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 19. 1 & 27. 17. Chap. 23. 1[illegible]

Or, bound.

t Whereby the Lands of several possessors were distinguished and divided. Do not enrich thy self with the injury of other men: Do not invade the rights of others.

entries.title: Proverbs 22:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u Or, expeditious, as the word properly signifies, one of quick dispatch, vigorous and speedy in executing what hath been well and wisely contrived.

x He is fit to be employed in the affairs of the greatest Princes.

Heb. obsc[illegible] men.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a When thou art invited to a Feast with a great man.

b Either 1. What person or persons. Or rather 2. What things, what plenty and variety of meats and drinks, by which thou maist easily be tempted to excess, and by that means induced to use such speeches or carriages, as may be unfit for thee, or many ways hurtful to thee.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Restrain and moderate thine appetite, as if a knife, or some other thing stuck in thy throat, and hindred thee from swallowing what thou didst desire; or, as if a man stood with a knife at thy Throat ready to kill thee, if thou didst transgress; or, though it be as irksom to thee to do so, as if thou hadst a knife put to thy Throat. So this is to be understood metaphorically, as that Phrase of cutting off the right hand, &c. Mat. 5. 29, 30. Or, For thou dost (or, left thou shouldst, as the Syriack Interpreter renders it; or, otherwise thou wiltst or shouldst) put a knife to thy throat. So the sense is, when thou goest to their Feasts, thou dost expose thy self to great and manifest hazards, to thy own intemperance, and to all its dangerous consequences, and to the ill effects of other mens intemperance.

d Prone to excess in eating and drinking.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: e Either because they do not yield thee that satisfaction which thou didst expect from them, but rather load thee with ill humors & the seeds of divers diseases; or because they are not provided for thee with sincerity and good Will, but with some evil design upon thee, either to discover and betray thee, or to enslave thee See below v. 6, 7.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 28. 20 1 Tim. 6. 9 10.

f Heb. Do not weary thy self with immoderate cares and labors, as many covetous men do.

g From that carnal Wisdom which is natural to man in his corrupt estate, which persuades men to believe that it is their interest to use all possible means to get Riches, and that the happiness of their Lives consists in the abundance of their Possessions, directly contrary to the assertion of our blessed Lord, Luke 12 15.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. [illegible] thou cause [illegible] eyes to fly [illegible]

h i. e. Look upon it [illegible] [illegible] and greedy desire, employing the Eyes of thy [illegible] and Body about it.

i Which hath no solid and setled being, which is ours to have, but not to hold, which is always upon the wing, and oft times gone in the twinkling of an Eye, so that the owner is frequently at a loss, and cannot tell whether he hath his Estate, or whether he hath lost it.

k Swiftly, strongly, and irrevocably. We quickly lose the sight and possession of them. Their flying away from us is elegantly opposed to our Eyes, being set, or, as it is in the Hebrew, flying upon them in the beginning of the verse.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: l Of the envious or covetous man, who secretly grudgeth thee the meat which he sets before thee, as this Phrase is used, Prov. 28. 22. Mat. 20. 15. as on the contrary a liberal man is said to have a good Eye, Prov. 22. 9.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m You are not to judge of him by his words, for so he prosesseth kindness, as it follows, but by the constant temper of his mind, which he hath fully discovered to all that know him by the course of his Life.

n He hath no sincere kindness to thee, but inwardly grudgeth thee that which he outwardly offers to thee.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o When thou perceivest his churlish disposition and carriage, his meat will be loathsom to thee, and thou wiltst wish either that thou hadst never eaten it, or that thou couldst vomit it up again.

p Thy pleasant discourse wherewith thou didst adorn his Table, and design both to delight and profit him, is lost, and of no effect to him, and thou wiltst be ready to repent of it.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 9. 8.

q Cast not away good Counsels upon obstinate and incorrigible sinners. We have the same advice given Mat. 7. 6.

r He will scornfully reject thy wise and good admonitions.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 19. 14. [illegible] 27. 17.

[illegible]. 22. 28. [illegible], bound.

s Either to take away their goods; or rather to possess their Lands, as this Phrase is used, 2 Sam. 5. 6.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 31. 21. [illegible]. 22. 23.

t Heb. their near kinsman, to whom it belongs to avenge their wrongs, and to recover and maintain their rights, of which see Lev. 25. 25. Numb. 35. 12. Thus God is pleased to call himself, to shew how much he concerns himself for the relief of oppressed and helpless persons.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: u Content not thy self with outward hearing or reading of it, but affectionately receive it into thine heart, and lay it up there as choice Treasure.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 13. 24. [illegible] 19. 18. [illegible] 22. 15. [illegible] 29. 15, 17.

x It is a likely mean to prevent their corruption, and the destruction which commonly follows it, as the next verse explains this.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y In the good success of my Counsels, and in thy Piety and Happiness, which is as truly desirable and pleasant to me, as my own.

Or, [illegible] I [illegible] rejoice.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: z I shall rejoice not onely in shew and profession, but inwardly, and with all my soul.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 37. 1. [illegible] [illegible]. 3. [illegible]. 3. 31. [illegible] [illegible]4. 1.

a Let not the consideration of their present impunity and prosperity stir thee up, either to envy them, or to approve and imitate their evil courses.

b Reverence the presence of the Divine Majesty, and dread his power and justice, and those judgments which he hath prepared for sinners, and thou wil[illegible]t see no cause to envy, but rather to [illegible] them.

c Not only when thou art in trouble, but in all times and conditions.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 24. 14.

Or, reward.

d An expected and happy end for such as fear God, which was required v. 17. Or, a reward, as this Hebrew word is rendred, Prov. 24. 20.

e Thou shalt certainly enjoy that good which thou expectest, as the wicked shall lose that Happiness which they enjoy.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Rest not in hearing, but see that thou growest wiser and better by it.

g Order the whole course of thine affections and actions.

h In Gods way, oft called the way, as hath been observed before.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 5 22. Luke 21. 34. Rom. 13. 13. Eph. 5. 18.

i Avoid their conversation and company, lest thou be either insected or injured by them.

Heb. of their flesh.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: k Immoderate sleep, and idleness, which is as ready a way to Poverty, as Gluttony or Drunkenness is.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 1. 8.

l And therefore desires and seeks thy good in all his counsels.

m When the infirmity of age is added to that of her sex, which is apt to breed contempt.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 4. 5, 7.

n Purchase it upon any terms, spare no pains nor cost to get it.

o The true and saving knowledg of Gods Mind and Will concerning your Salvation, and the way that leads to it.

p Do not forget it, nor forsake it for any worldly advantages, as ungodly men frequently do.

q Whereby you may love and practise the truth known and received.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
r He repeateth this again as a powerful Argument to prevail with all Children, that are not void of natural affection to labour to be wise and good, that so they may glad the hearts of their Parents to whom they have such high and indelible obligations.

s With so great pain and hazard, and brought thee up with such tender care, whom thou canst not better require.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:26
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t Receive my Counsels with thy whole heart. Selomon speaking in Gods Name, and cause, requires the heart to be given to him.

u Let thy mind seriously and practically consider.

x Either 1. The ways in which I have walked, my evil practices: take warning by my sad example. Or 2. The ways which I prescribe to you, as the Apostles called the Gospel which they preached, their Gospel, 1 Thes. 1. 5. 2 Tim. 2. 8.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:27
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 22. 14.

y In which a man is in evident danger of perdition, and out of which it is exceeding difficult to escape.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:28
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Chap. 7. 12.

Or, as a robber.

z Watching all opportunities of ensnaring young men to their destruction.

a She is the cause of innumerable sins against God, and against the MarriageBed, against the Soul and Body too, and by her wicked Example and Arts, involveth many persons in the guilt of her sins.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:29
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Isa. 5. 11, 22.

b From the [illegible] of Lust he proceeds to that of drunkenness, which doth frequently accompany it.

c The sin of much and impertinent talking: or, [illegible] noise or clamour, which is usual among Drunkards. See [illegible]. 20. 1.

d Upon every sleight occasion, which men enflamed with Wine are very apt to take.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:30
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: e Either mixed with Water, or with other ingredients to make it strong and delicious. Heb. mixture, mixed drinks of several sorts suited to their Palats.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:31
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Earnestly, so as to inflame thine Appetite towards it, in which sense men are forbidden to look upon a Woman, Job 31. 1. Mat. 5. 28.

g Which was the colour of the best Wines in that Countrey, which therefore are called Blood, Gen. 49. 11. Deut. 32. 14. and such were used by them in the Passover.

Cant. 7. 9.

h When it sparkleth and frisketh, and seems to smile upon a Man.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:32
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, a Cockatrice.

i It hurts the Body in many respects, impairs the vigor of the Mind, wastes the Estate and Reputation, wounds the Conscience, and without Repentance, will destroy the Soul.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:33
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k With evil intent, or lustfully, which is the effect of drinking much Wine, as is noted in Scripture, Gen. 19. 31, 35. Hos. 4. 18. and other Authors.

l Thine Heart, which when thou hadst the use of thy wit, concealed, will then discover its wickedness, by filthy and perverse speeches.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:34
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m To sleep, of which that word is frequently used.

Heb. in the heart of the Sea.

n In a Ship in the midst of the Sea, This Phrase notes the temper and condition of the Drunkard, the giddiness of his Brain, the unquietness of his Mind, and especially his extream danger joyned with great security.

o The worst part of the Ship, both for its perpetual tossings, and for the hazard of him that sleeps in it.

entries.title: Proverbs 23:35
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p I cannot deny that I exposed my self by my Drunkenness to manifold abuses and injuries.

q I was not then sensible of it, neither do I now find any great hurt by it; it was but the effect of a present frolick, at which I have no cause to be much troubled.

Heb. I knew it not.

r At present I find some inconvenience, and my condition requires sleep to settle my self, and when I am composed and refreshed, I purpose to return to my former course. But that which Solomon here expresseth, seems rather to be the Language of their Hearts or Lives, than of their actions. Compare Prov. 1. 11.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 37. 1. &c. & 73. 3. Ch. 3. 31. & 23. 17. Vers. 19.

a Their Company or manner of life.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 10. 7.

b How they may oppress and destroy others, which yet at last falls upon their own heads.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: c There is no need that thou shouldst raise thy Self and Family by ruining others, as the manner of wicked men is, which thou maist more easily and effectually do by Wisdom, and the fear of God.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: d Which in Scripture Phrase includes the love and practice of that which we know.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 21. 22. Eccles. 9. 16.

Heb. is in strength.

e Is couragious and resolute, and able by Wisdom to do greater things than others can accomplish by their own strength.

Heb. strengtheneth might.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ch. 11. 14. & 15. 22. & 20. 18.

f War is better managed by Wisdom than by strength So this proves what he said in the last Verse.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Either 1. really, it is above his reach or capacity. Or 2. in his opinion; he judgeth it too hard for him, he despairs of attaining it, he pretends the impossibility of it, because he will not put himself to the charge or trouble of getting it: as on the contrary Wisdom is said to be easie to him that understandeth, Prov. 14. 6. because he seriously giveth his mind to it, and therefore easily and certainly attains to it.

h For a wilful Fool, or a wicked Man, whose lusts enfeeble and darken his Mind, and make it uncapable of Wisdom.

i Either 1. he can say nothing for himself when he is accused before the Magistrate, for which he gives frequent occasion. Or 2. he knows not how to speak acceptably, and profitably in the publick Assembly among wise men.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: k Heb. a Master of mischief. The sense is, Though he cover his wicked devices with fair pretences and would be better esteemed, yet he shall be noted and branded with that infamy which is due to him.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
l The very inward thought or contrivance of evil, of which he spake, v. 8. even before it break forth into action, is a sin in God's sight, and it is hateful to God. Or, foolishness is put for foolish or wicked men, by comparing this with the next clause where the scorner is opposed to it. So the sense is, All the Thoughts of wicked men are onely evil and that continually, as is said of man in his corrupt estate, Gen. 6. 5. and therefore abominable to God.

Or, but.

m He who not onely deviseth and practiseth wickedness, but obstinately persists in it, and rejects all admonitions against it.

n Is abominable not onely to God, as all sinners are, but to all sober men.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o If thou art impatient and unable to bear sufferings, if thy resolution flag, and thou givest way to despondency or dejection of Mind.

Heb. [illegible] row.

p Heb. is narrow, it lives in a little compass, it is as strait as thy condition is; for there is an Elegant allusion in the Hebrew words. The sense is, This is a sign that thou hast but little Christian strength or courage, for that is best known by adversity.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Ps. 82. 4.

q When it is in thy power to do it lawfully.

r To wit, unjustly or by the violence of lawless men.

s That are in present danger of Death or Destruction.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, him.

t I was ignorant either of his innocency, or of his extream danger, or of my power to relieve him.

u That this is onely a frivolous excuse, and that the true reason of thy neglect was thy want of true love to thy Brother, whose life thou wast by the Law of God, and of Nature obliged to preserve, and thy sinful selflove, and a carnal fear of some mischief for trouble which might befal thee in the discharge of thy duty.

x God who is the preserver of men, Job 7. 20. who daily doth and who onely can keep thee both in and from the greatest dangers. And this favour of God may be here mentioned partly as a strong Obligation upon him to preserve him who is made after God's Image, and whom God hath commanded him to love and preserve; partly as an encouragement to the performance of his duty herein from the consideration of God's special care and watchfulness over those that do their duty; and partly to intimate to them the danger of the neglect of this duty whereby they will forfeit God's protection over themselves, and expose themselves to manifold dangers and calamities. Or, as others render it, and as the Hebrew Verb is frequently used, he that observeth thy Soul, that seeth all the secret Thoughts and inward motions of the Heart. Which exposition is favoured both by the following words, Doth not he know it? Which agrees better to God's observing than to his preserving a Man's So[illegible] and by the former clause, to which this Translation doth more exactly answer, the same thing being here repeated in other words, after the manner of these Sacred Writers.

Job 34. 11. Ps. 62. 12. Jer. 32. 19. Rom. 2. 6. Rev. [illegible]. 12.

y God will certainly deal with thee as thou hast dealt with him, either rewarding thy performance of this duty, or punishing thy neglect of it.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
z This is not a command but a corcession, and is here expressed onely to illustrate the following Verse. Honey in those parts was excellent, and an usual and acceptable food. See Deut. 8. 8. Iudg. 14. 18. 1 Sam. 14. 25.

Heb. [illegible] thy Palate.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 10. [illegible] 103.

a Whereby he implies that there is indeed some difficulty and trouble in the pursuit of Wisdom, but that it is abundantly compensated with the sweetness and advantage of it when a Man arrives at it.

[illegible]. 18.

b Heb. and, or also there is a reward. It is not onely as good as hony, sweet for the present, but it is infinitely better, bringing a sure and everlasting reward with it.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Do him no injury either by subtil and secret devices, or, as it follows, by manifest violence.

d Against his Person or Family or Possessions.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 19 [illegible] 19.

e Either 1. into sin. Or rather 2. into calamities, of which he evidently speaks both in the foregoing Verse, and in the opposite and following branch of this Verse, and so this word is used in the next Verse, and Psal. 37. 24. Isa. 24. [illegible]0. Ier. 25. 27. Amos 8. 14. Mic. 7. 8, &c. And so this is fitly alledged as a just reason to distuade wicked Men from their unjust attempts against righteous men, because they should not succeed in them, and although they might, by God's permission, bring them into some distress for a time, yet God would deliver them out of their hands, and they should be disappointed of their hopes.

f i. e. Frequently.

[illegible] [illegible] 5. 2.

g Into unavoidable and irrecoverable destruction, oft-times in this life, and infallibly in the next.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:17
